title: Proxmox VE 9 high availability: HA rules, fencing and a failover you have actually tested
summary: High availability is the feature most people build a Proxmox VE cluster for: a node dies at 3 a.m. and its important guests are running again on another node before anyone wakes up. Proxmox VE does this with two daemons, a watchdog and a set of rules. This post explains how those pieces fit together, adds guests to HA, writes placement rules (which changed in Proxmox VE 9), walks through a node failure step by step, and covers planned shutdowns and maintenance. The trap HA gets switched on for a cluster that is not ready for it: two nodes and no QDevice, or guests whose disks live on local storage with no replica. When a node fails, nothing restarts, or the surviving node fences itself. The second trap is using HA as a substitute for backups. HA restarts the guest. It does not undo whatever was wrong with it. The documented requirements are short: at least three cluster nodes (or two plus a QDevice) for reliable quorum, shared storage for the guests (or replicated storage, with a data-loss window back to the last replica), hardware redundancy, and a watchdog. The HA stack in two daemons Every node runs: pve-ha-lrm , the local resource manager. It starts and stops HA guests on its own node, following the state the CRM requests. pve-ha-crm , the cluster resource manager. One node's CRM is the active master at any time. It tells the LRMs what to run, moves guests when something fails and handles fencing. Both rely on locks in the cluster file system and on a watchdog . While a node is healthy and quorate, its daemons keep resetting the watchdog timer. If the node loses quorum or the HA daemons stop working, the timer runs out and the watchdog resets the node. Why fencing matters Before a guest from a failed node can start somewhere else, the cluster must be certain the failed node is not still running it, perhaps cut off from the network but still writing to shared storage. Starting a second copy would corrupt the disk. Making sure the node is really off is called fencing. Proxmox VE fences with watchdog timers. A node outside the quorate part of the cluster cannot reset its watchdog, so the watchdog resets it. Once the CRM master can take the failed node's lock, it knows the node has fenced itself and can recover its guests. Without a configured hardware watchdog, Proxmox VE uses the Linux kernel's softdog , which the docs describe as reliable but not independent of the server's hardware. Hardware watchdog modules are blocked by default; to use one, name its module and reboot: # /etc/default/pve-ha-manager WATCHDOG_MODULE = iTCO_wdt One warning from the docs worth repeating: never kill pve-ha-crm , pve-ha-lrm or watchdog-mux by hand. They manage the watchdog, and killing them can cause an immediate reset of the node. Adding guests to HA An HA resource is a type and an ID: vm:100 , ct:110 . ha-manager add vm:100 ha-manager add ct:110 --state started --max_restart 1 --max_relocate 1 ha-manager config ha-manager status In the web interface it is Datacenter → HA → Resources → Add , or More → Manage HA on a guest. --state is the requested state: started , stopped , disabled or ignored . Once HA manages a guest, ordinary qm start and qm stop simply change its requested state. max_restart is how often HA retries starting it on the same node after a failed start, and max_relocate how often it tries another node; both default to 1. ha-manager set vm:100 --state stopped # stop and keep stopped ha-manager migrate vm:100 pve2 # live migration ha-manager relocate vm:100 pve2 # stop, move, start ha-manager remove vm:100 # stop managing (does not stop it) Before you add a guest, check it can run on every node HA might pick: disks on shared or replicated storage, bridges with the same names on every node, and no passthrough devices. If a dependency exists on only some nodes, restrict the guest to them with a strict node affinity rule. HA groups became HA rules in Proxmox VE 9 Earlier releases used HA groups to say which nodes a guest prefers. Proxmox VE 9.0 deprecated them in favour of HA rules , stored in /etc/pve/ha/rules.cfg . Existing groups are migrated to node affinity rules automatically once every node runs Proxmox VE 9; if anything looks wrong afterwards, the upgrade guide points to the active CRM's log, journalctl -eu pve-ha-crm . Node affinity: which nodes a guest runs on # Prefer pve1 for the firewall VM; any node is fine if pve1 is down ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \ --nodes pve1 # Make it a hard requirement instead ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1 # Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \ --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1" # Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node) ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \ --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3 Node affinity rules are not strict by default : if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback , a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns. Resource affinity: guests together or apart # Two DNS servers should never share a node ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \ --resources ct:120,ct:121 # An app and its database should stay together ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \ --resources vm:130,vm:131 Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes. Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit. What happens when a node dies Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate. The CRM master marks pve2 's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence ). If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice. Once the CRM can take pve2 's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery . The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it. With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA. Test it with the power cord Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy. Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg : ha: shutdown_policy=migrate conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node. migrate : mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back. failover : stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon. freeze : stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns. The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate : a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in. Maintenance mode for one node For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it: ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2 ha-manager status # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2 # ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ... ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2 It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it. For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze , then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short. Checklist Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice). Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage. Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts). The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident. A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded. Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node. This is adapted from my book Cluster Without Fear (Homelab the Right Way, Book 13). The free sample is here and the full book is here . summary_html:
High availability is the feature most people build a Proxmox VE cluster for: a node dies at 3 a.m. and its important guests are running again on another node before anyone wakes up. Proxmox VE does this with two daemons, a watchdog and a set of rules. This post explains how those pieces fit together, adds guests to HA, writes placement rules (which changed in Proxmox VE 9), walks through a node failure step by step, and covers planned shutdowns and maintenance.

The trap

HA gets switched on for a cluster that is not ready for it: two nodes and no QDevice, or guests whose disks live on local storage with no replica. When a node fails, nothing restarts, or the surviving node fences itself.

The second trap is using HA as a substitute for backups. HA restarts the guest. It does not undo whatever was wrong with it.

The documented requirements are short: at least three cluster nodes (or two plus a QDevice) for reliable quorum, shared storage for the guests (or replicated storage, with a data-loss window back to the last replica), hardware redundancy, and a watchdog.

The HA stack in two daemons

Every node runs:

  • pve-ha-lrm, the local resource manager. It starts and stops HA guests on its own node, following the state the CRM requests.
  • pve-ha-crm, the cluster resource manager. One node's CRM is the active master at any time. It tells the LRMs what to run, moves guests when something fails and handles fencing.

Both rely on locks in the cluster file system and on a watchdog. While a node is healthy and quorate, its daemons keep resetting the watchdog timer. If the node loses quorum or the HA daemons stop working, the timer runs out and the watchdog resets the node.

Why fencing matters

Before a guest from a failed node can start somewhere else, the cluster must be certain the failed node is not still running it, perhaps cut off from the network but still writing to shared storage. Starting a second copy would corrupt the disk. Making sure the node is really off is called fencing.

Proxmox VE fences with watchdog timers. A node outside the quorate part of the cluster cannot reset its watchdog, so the watchdog resets it. Once the CRM master can take the failed node's lock, it knows the node has fenced itself and can recover its guests.

Without a configured hardware watchdog, Proxmox VE uses the Linux kernel's softdog, which the docs describe as reliable but not independent of the server's hardware. Hardware watchdog modules are blocked by default; to use one, name its module and reboot:

# /etc/default/pve-ha-manager
WATCHDOG_MODULE=iTCO_wdt

One warning from the docs worth repeating: never kill pve-ha-crm, pve-ha-lrm or watchdog-mux by hand. They manage the watchdog, and killing them can cause an immediate reset of the node.

Adding guests to HA

An HA resource is a type and an ID: vm:100, ct:110.

ha-manager add vm:100
ha-manager add ct:110 --state started --max_restart 1 --max_relocate 1
ha-manager config
ha-manager status

In the web interface it is Datacenter → HA → Resources → Add, or More → Manage HA on a guest.

--state is the requested state: started, stopped, disabled or ignored. Once HA manages a guest, ordinary qm start and qm stop simply change its requested state. max_restart is how often HA retries starting it on the same node after a failed start, and max_relocate how often it tries another node; both default to 1.

ha-manager set vm:100 --state stopped     # stop and keep stopped
ha-manager migrate vm:100 pve2            # live migration
ha-manager relocate vm:100 pve2           # stop, move, start
ha-manager remove vm:100                  # stop managing (does not stop it)

Before you add a guest, check it can run on every node HA might pick: disks on shared or replicated storage, bridges with the same names on every node, and no passthrough devices. If a dependency exists on only some nodes, restrict the guest to them with a strict node affinity rule.

HA groups became HA rules in Proxmox VE 9

Earlier releases used HA groups to say which nodes a guest prefers. Proxmox VE 9.0 deprecated them in favour of HA rules, stored in /etc/pve/ha/rules.cfg. Existing groups are migrated to node affinity rules automatically once every node runs Proxmox VE 9; if anything looks wrong afterwards, the upgrade guide points to the active CRM's log, journalctl -eu pve-ha-crm.

Node affinity: which nodes a guest runs on 
# Prefer pve1 for the firewall VM; any node is fine if pve1 is down
ha-manager rules add node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --resources vm:100 \
  --nodes pve1
# Make it a hard requirement instead
ha-manager rules set node-affinity fw-on-pve1 --strict 1
# Ordered preference: pve1 first, then pve2 or pve3 equally
ha-manager rules add node-affinity ha-core \
  --resources vm:101,ct:110 --nodes "pve1:2,pve2:1,pve3:1"
# Keep these guests off pve3 (the small node)
ha-manager rules add node-affinity not-pve3 --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:200,vm:300 --nodes pve3

Node affinity rules are not strict by default: if none of the listed nodes is available, the guest may run elsewhere. With --strict 1 it is restricted to the listed nodes and stopped if none of them is up. Priorities are relative; higher numbers win, and nodes without a number get 0. failback, a per-resource property that defaults to on, moves a guest back to its highest-priority node when that node returns.

Resource affinity: guests together or apart 
# Two DNS servers should never share a node
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity dns-apart --affinity negative \
  --resources ct:120,ct:121
# An app and its database should stay together
ha-manager rules add resource-affinity app-with-db --affinity positive \
  --resources vm:130,vm:131

Resource affinity rules are the opposite: strict by default. A negative rule cannot list more resources than there are nodes.

Rules are checked for conflicts before they apply. A resource can be in only one node affinity rule, for example, and two resources cannot be kept both together and apart. A conflicting rule is disabled until you resolve it, so run ha-manager rules config after every edit.

What happens when a node dies
  1. Node pve2 loses power. Corosync on pve1 and pve3 stops hearing from it and forms a new membership without it. Two of three votes: still quorate.
  2. The CRM master marks pve2's HA guests as waiting for fencing (state fence).
  3. If pve2 were still running but cut off, it would be in a minority without quorum and unable to reset its watchdog, and the watchdog (60 seconds, per the docs) would reset it. A node with no power is already fenced in practice.
  4. Once the CRM can take pve2's lock, the node counts as fenced and its guests move to recovery.
  5. The CRM picks a node for each guest from the online, quorate nodes, narrowed by the affinity rules, and chooses the one with the lowest load. The guests start there.
  6. When pve2 comes back it rejoins the cluster, and guests with failback move back if a rule prefers it.

With Ceph or shared storage the guests start with every completed write intact. With ZFS replication they start from the last replica. And every guest that ran on the failed node now runs on fewer nodes, which the docs warn can overload small clusters: size each node so the others can carry its HA guests, or mark only what truly matters as HA.

Test it with the power cord

Before you trust HA with the firewall, test it with a disposable VM: add it to HA, then pull the power cord (not a clean shutdown) of the node running it. Watch ha-manager status on another node until the VM shows as started on its new home. A clean shutdown tests something else, the shutdown policy.

Planned shutdowns: pick a shutdown policy

A planned shutdown is not a failure, and HA handles it according to the cluster's shutdown policy, set in Datacenter → Options → HA Settings or in datacenter.cfg:

ha: shutdown_policy=migrate
  • conditional (the default): on shutdown, stop the guests and let other nodes take them over; on reboot, freeze them and start them again on the same node.
  • migrate: mark the node unavailable and live-migrate its HA guests away first; they return when it is back.
  • failover: stop the guests and recover them elsewhere if the node is not back soon.
  • freeze: stop and freeze the guests; nothing moves until the node returns.

The docs note that conditional is the default for backward compatibility and that some users find migrate behaves more as expected. One catch with migrate: a guest restricted by a strict node affinity rule to unavailable nodes makes the shutdown hang until you step in.

Maintenance mode for one node

For work on a single node, maintenance mode is the cleanest tool. It migrates the node's HA guests away and brings them back when you disable it:

ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance enable pve2
ha-manager status          # wait until no HA guests remain on pve2
# ... patch, reboot, replace hardware ...
ha-manager crm-command node-maintenance disable pve2

It can run from any node. The LRM shows maintenance as soon as the request is picked up, before every guest has moved, so watch the guest list rather than the status word. Maintenance mode survives a reboot and ends only when you disable it.

For work that could briefly break quorum everywhere, such as re-cabling the corosync network, Proxmox VE 9.2 added a cluster-wide switch: ha-manager crm-command disarm-ha freeze, then ha-manager crm-command arm-ha when you are done. While HA is disarmed it protects nothing, so keep the window short.

Checklist
  • Quorum survives one node down (three nodes, or two plus a QDevice).
  • Every HA guest's disks are on shared, Ceph or replicated storage.
  • Every rule in ha-manager rules config is enabled (no conflicts).
  • The shutdown policy is a deliberate choice, not the default by accident.
  • A pulled-power failover test of a disposable VM succeeded.
  • Each node can carry the HA guests of any one failed node.

title: What Is d3kOS?
summary: The Marine Operating System Built for the Future Your phone has an operating system. So does your laptop, your car's infotainment screen and your TV. Boats are the exception. A modern recreational boat can carry a chartplotter, a depth sounder, engine gauges, an AIS receiver, a VHF radio, cameras and a stereo, and almost none of them talk to each other in a way the owner can use. d3kOS was built to change that. It is an open-source marine operating system that runs on a Raspberry Pi at the helm and turns the data already on your boat into one connected, intelligent system. Engine data is on one screen, the chart on another, and cameras somewhere else. Closed ecosystems. Many devices only share data fully with equipment from the same manufacturer. Data with no context. The engine sensor knows the coolant temperature, but nothing on the boat knows whether that temperature is normal for this engine at this RPM . No single place to ask a question. If you want to know what a warning means, you usually have to dig through a paper manual. The data exists. What's missing is a layer that collects it, makes sense of it and presents it in one place. Why Boats Need an Operating System An operating system does three jobs: it manages hardware, runs applications, and gives the user one consistent interface. A vessel operating system does the same for a boat: Manages hardware: GPS receivers, NMEA 2000 adapters, AIS receivers, IP cameras, microphones and speakers. Runs marine applications: charts, engine monitoring, anchor watch, collision advisory, voice assistance and logging. Gives one interface: a single touchscreen dashboard at the helm, plus remote access from a phone. d3kOS ships as a complete image for the SD card. You flash it, boot the Pi, and a setup wizard walks you through configuring the vessel. No programming is needed after installation. What d3kOS Includes Today The current release (v0.9.9.5.1, October 2026) provides these tools on the helm touchscreen: ToolWhat it does* AI Navigation Ask plain-English questions about navigation, regulations or a route Engine Dashboard Live RPM, coolant temperature, oil pressure, battery voltage and fuel level, with alerts Helm Assistant Hands-free voice AI. Say "Helm" and ask a question Anchor Watch Sounds an alarm if the boat drifts beyond a set radius Marine Vision Connects up to 20 IP cameras, with fish detection for fishing boats SafeHelm Collision-avoidance advisory using AIS targets and COLREGs logic Boat Log Automatic trip log of engine starts and stops, position snapshots and voice notes Upload Documents Load your engine manual or checklists so Helm can answer from your own documents Charts and Weather *AvNav chart plotter and a live wind and wave map built into the dashboard d3kOS supports 18 display languages and runs on the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4B and 5 (4 GB RAM minimum). Signal K Integration: The Data Foundation d3kOS is built on Signal K , the open marine data standard. Signal K takes data from NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 devices and turns it into a consistent, web-friendly JSON data model. Every value, whether speed over ground, depth or engine RPM, has a predictable address and consistent units. This is why d3kOS works with existing equipment instead of replacing it. Every automated action follows the AAO methodology , a framework that limits what AI is allowed to do, logs every action and guarantees recovery. It is an aid to awareness and does not replace proper seamanship, certified charts, a proper lookout, or the equipment the law requires. AI answers can be wrong. Never rely on them for safety-critical decisions. Frequently Asked Questions Is d3kOS open source? Yes. d3kOS is released under the GNU GPL v3. A separate commercial licence is available for bundling it with hardware for resale. Does d3kOS replace my chartplotter? No. d3kOS works alongside your existing electronics. It reads their data through Signal K and adds intelligence on top. Does d3kOS need the internet? No. Core functions work offline. An internet connection adds Gemini AI answers, weather maps and remote access. Who supports d3kOS? AtMyBoat.com is the community and support platform for d3kOS. It provides the mobile companion app, the Fix My Pi diagnostics and a community forum.
summary_html:
The Marine Operating System Built for the Future

Your phone has an operating system. So does your laptop, your car's infotainment screen and your TV. Boats are the exception. A modern recreational boat can carry a chartplotter, a depth sounder, engine gauges, an AIS receiver, a VHF radio, cameras and a stereo, and almost none of them talk to each other in a way the owner can use.

d3kOS was built to change that. It is an open-source marine operating system that runs on a Raspberry Pi at the helm and turns the data already on your boat into one connected, intelligent system.

The Problem with Today's Marine Technology

Marine electronics have grown one box at a time. Each device solves one problem well, but together they leave the boater with:

  • Fragmented displays. Engine data is on one screen, the chart on another, and cameras somewhere else.

  • Closed ecosystems. Many devices only share data fully with equipment from the same manufacturer.

  • Data with no context. The engine sensor knows the coolant temperature, but nothing on the boat knows whether that temperature is normal for this engine at this RPM.

  • No single place to ask a question. If you want to know what a warning means, you usually have to dig through a paper manual.

The data exists. What's missing is a layer that collects it, makes sense of it and presents it in one place.

Why Boats Need an Operating System

An operating system does three jobs: it manages hardware, runs applications, and gives the user one consistent interface. A vessel operating system does the same for a boat:

  • Manages hardware: GPS receivers, NMEA 2000 adapters, AIS receivers, IP cameras, microphones and speakers.

  • Runs marine applications: charts, engine monitoring, anchor watch, collision advisory, voice assistance and logging.

  • Gives one interface: a single touchscreen dashboard at the helm, plus remote access from a phone.

d3kOS ships as a complete image for the SD card. You flash it, boot the Pi, and a setup wizard walks you through configuring the vessel. No programming is needed after installation.

What d3kOS Includes Today

The current release (v0.9.9.5.1, October 2026) provides these tools on the helm touchscreen:

ToolWhat it does*AI NavigationAsk plain-English questions about navigation, regulations or a routeEngine DashboardLive RPM, coolant temperature, oil pressure, battery voltage and fuel level, with alertsHelm AssistantHands-free voice AI. Say "Helm" and ask a questionAnchor WatchSounds an alarm if the boat drifts beyond a set radiusMarine VisionConnects up to 20 IP cameras, with fish detection for fishing boatsSafeHelmCollision-avoidance advisory using AIS targets and COLREGs logicBoat LogAutomatic trip log of engine starts and stops, position snapshots and voice notesUpload DocumentsLoad your engine manual or checklists so Helm can answer from your own documentsCharts and Weather*AvNav chart plotter and a live wind and wave map built into the dashboard

d3kOS supports 18 display languages and runs on the Raspberry Pi 3B+, 4B and 5 (4 GB RAM minimum).

Signal K Integration: The Data Foundation

d3kOS is built on Signal K, the open marine data standard. Signal K takes data from NMEA 0183 and NMEA 2000 devices and turns it into a consistent, web-friendly JSON data model. Every value, whether speed over ground, depth or engine RPM, has a predictable address and consistent units.

This is why d3kOS works with existing equipment instead of replacing it. Your chartplotter, depth sounder and engine sensors keep doing their jobs. d3kOS reads what they already broadcast. (See How Signal K and d3kOS Create the Digital Vessel.)

AI-Native Architecture

Most marine software adds AI as an afterthought. d3kOS was designed around it from the start:

  • Helm voice assistant. On-device speech recognition (Vosk) and speech synthesis (Piper), with the Gemini language model for answers when a connection is available.

  • Retrieval from your own manuals. Upload a PDF and Helm can answer questions from it.

  • Offline fallback. With no internet, Helm still answers from its local knowledge base. That matters on the water, where connectivity is never guaranteed.

  • Computer vision. The Forward Watch plugin uses a custom-trained YOLOv8 model to detect ships, boats, buoys, kayaks, logs and debris from a bow camera.

  • Governed autonomy. Every automated action follows the AAO methodology, a framework that limits what AI is allowed to do, logs every action and guarantees recovery.

Built to Stay Current

d3kOS updates itself over the air. Updates are signed packages that are checked with an ECDSA signature and a SHA-256 integrity check before they install. If a health check fails afterwards, the update rolls back automatically, and the installer refuses to "update" to an older version. You don't need to swap SD cards or open a terminal.

Future Roadmap

The d3kOS roadmap is driven by real on-water testing. Areas in active development include:

  • More Forward Watch model training on real-world marine footage

  • Expanded SafeHelm collision-avoidance capability

  • More engine-sensor integration options for boats without NMEA 2000 engine data

  • Research into short-range proximity sensing for small craft

Important Safety Note

d3kOS is not a certified navigation instrument. It is an aid to awareness and does not replace proper seamanship, certified charts, a proper lookout, or the equipment the law requires. AI answers can be wrong. Never rely on them for safety-critical decisions.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is d3kOS open source? Yes. d3kOS is released under the GNU GPL v3. A separate commercial licence is available for bundling it with hardware for resale.

Does d3kOS replace my chartplotter? No. d3kOS works alongside your existing electronics. It reads their data through Signal K and adds intelligence on top.

Does d3kOS need the internet? No. Core functions work offline. An internet connection adds Gemini AI answers, weather maps and remote access.

Who supports d3kOS? AtMyBoat.com is the community and support platform for d3kOS. It provides the mobile companion app, the Fix My Pi diagnostics and a community forum.

title: Hreflang Routes International URLs, but It Does Not Make Them Rank
summary: Hreflang is often treated as an international SEO ranking tactic. Google’s newer framing points to a more useful interpretation: hreflang helps the search engine understand and route between alternate versions of a page, but it does not make those pages rank better on its own. That distinction matters for businesses operating multilingual or multi-market websites. A regional URL can be a valid alternate in a hreflang cluster even when Google has not independently indexed it as the main representative of that cluster. The practical question is no longer simply whether every market has a URL. It is whether each market page gives users, and increasingly AI-driven retrieval systems, a meaningful reason to select it. Hreflang is a relationship signal, not a ranking signal In Bill Hunt’s analysis for Search Engine Journal , hreflang is described through Google’s emerging “alternate names” mental model. The idea is that localized or regional versions are connected representations of substantially the same underlying content. Google can use that relationship to serve the appropriate version to a user based on language, region, device, or other context. This is different from treating each alternate URL as a separately competing ranking asset. Google’s own Alternate URLs help documentation similarly explains that alternate URLs may be served for language or device and can include unmarked duplicates. In this model, an alternate can be useful to serve even when it is not the URL Google has chosen to represent the duplicate cluster in its index. The consequence is straightforward: correctly implemented hreflang can reduce ambiguity about which localized version belongs with which page, but it does not create a direct ranking advantage. It cannot compensate for weak relevance, poor technical accessibility, or near-identical market pages with little user value. Discovery, indexing, and serving are not the same process The key insight in the “alternate names” framing is that discovery, indexing, and serving can be separated. A site may publish many localized URLs and connect them correctly with hreflang. Google can discover those URLs and understand their relationship. It may then cluster them as duplicates or near-duplicates and select one version as the indexed representative. Later, it can still serve a different alternate from the same cluster when that version better matches a searcher’s language or market context. Hunt illustrates the concept with a common international SEO challenge: a company maintains versions of one product page across dozens of markets, while most of the on-page information remains the same. Google does not necessarily need to index every version independently to understand the product and its alternates. It can consolidate similar pages while retaining the ability to route users to an appropriate local URL. This helps explain why an SEO team should not use an individual URL’s apparent indexing status as the only measure of whether hreflang is working. A URL may still have a role in a language or regional cluster. At the same time, being included in a cluster should not be mistaken for evidence that the page has earned visibility for competitive queries. Why distinct market content matters more For international sites, the important strategic shift is from URL coverage to market differentiation. A translated page can be necessary for users, compliance, and local conversion. But translation alone does not automatically establish a separate search value proposition. When pages are substantively equivalent, Google has a rational basis to cluster them. In AI-heavy search experiences and semantic retrieval systems, equivalent meaning can also be recognized across languages more readily than marketers may expect. That raises the standard for localized content. A market page is more likely to offer distinct value when it addresses real local differences, such as: Country-specific regulations, eligibility, or product restrictions. Local prices, currencies, taxes, delivery terms, or availability. Regionally relevant use cases, examples, terminology, and customer concerns. Local support arrangements, contact details, or service coverage. Market-specific product configurations, specifications, or legal information. These differences are not merely SEO embellishments. They can make a page more useful to the intended audience and clarify why it should be treated as more than a duplicate representation of a global template. What this means for AI search visibility Hreflang remains important in an AI-influenced search environment, but its role is foundational rather than promotional. It helps systems interpret which versions are intended alternatives. It does not by itself make a brand more likely to be cited, recommended, or selected in an AI-generated response. For that, the underlying content still needs to be accessible, specific, and relevant to the query. A page describing local eligibility requirements or locally available product options has clearer evidence to contribute than a regional URL that repeats a generic global description. This does not mean every market needs wholly original editorial content. It means teams should be deliberate about where genuine differences exist and represent those differences accurately. Artificially rewriting identical content simply to appear unique can create maintenance burdens without improving usefulness. A practical audit for international websites Start by reviewing market pages in groups , not as isolated URLs. For each product, service, category, or editorial page, ask whether the regional variants genuinely differ in ways that matter to users. Then review the technical implementation . Google’s localized versions guidance remains the reference point for implementing hreflang annotations. Ensure intended alternates are connected consistently and that language and regional targeting reflect the actual page audience. A useful audit should separate three questions: Relationship: Are the alternate URLs correctly declared and mutually connected where appropriate? Accessibility: Can Google discover and crawl the pages without avoidable technical barriers? Differentiation: Does each market page contain accurate local information that justifies its existence for users? The third question is often the most important strategic one. If a market version has no material local distinction, it may still be appropriate as an alternate for users. But teams should not expect hreflang alone to make it independently competitive in search results. If your international pages are largely template-driven, create a GEO Search Leads account to begin assessing where your website’s content may need clearer market-specific signals. A structured review can help identify opportunities to make localized pages more useful for real customer questions while keeping technical relationships and content strategy aligned. Frequently Asked Questions Does hreflang improve rankings? No. Hreflang helps Google understand language and regional alternatives, but it is not a direct ranking signal. Ranking still depends on the relevance, quality, accessibility, and usefulness of the underlying content. Can Google serve a hreflang URL that is not independently indexed? According to the alternate URL model discussed in the source material, Google can cluster similar URLs, index one representative, and serve an appropriate alternate URL for a relevant language or regional context. Should every country have its own page? Not automatically. Separate pages make sense when they serve users in a language or market and accurately reflect local needs. Their value is stronger when they include meaningful differences such as availability, regulations, pricing, or local use cases. Is hreflang still important for AI search? Yes, as a way to clarify the relationship between localized alternatives. However, hreflang does not itself create AI visibility. Market-specific, useful content remains the stronger basis for retrieval, citations, and recommendations. Conclusion Hreflang is best understood as a routing and relationship mechanism, not a shortcut to higher rankings. International SEO teams should maintain accurate alternate annotations, while investing their main effort in content that reflects real differences between markets. That combination gives search systems clearer technical context and gives users a stronger reason to choose the local page.

title: MiniMax H3 Action Director: One Graph, Three Modes, Nine LoRA Presets
summary: The useful starting point for this action-video workflow is not its most dramatic promotional claim. It is the control panel: which generation mode is selected, which prompt belongs to that mode, and which LoRA coefficients actually reach the model? The supplied MiniMax H3 Action Director export is one workflow with 95 nodes and 160 links . Its nine presets are arithmetic recipes inside that graph, not nine independent workflow files. It supports three intended input routes and an optional latent-refinement path. This walkthrough follows the saved configuration; it does not report a new video render, successful character match, or verified action-contact result. Prepare the exact dependencies Both base-model loaders select minimax_h3_fl2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors . The reference branch adds minimax_h3_ref_lora_layer20-49adaln_proj_rank_256_bf16.safetensors before its action LoRAs. It does not select a separate Ref2VA checkpoint in this export. Other common loader references are: qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors , with encoder type minimax ; minimax_h3_video_vae_int8_convrot.safetensors ; minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors . The five action-LoRA filenames are H3_Combat_V2.safetensors , Bunny_weapon_combatV1.safetensors , GunFu.safetensors , Motion_Repair_V2.safetensors , and H3_Fight_Flow_V1.safetensors . Optional refinement also references minimax_h3_latent_upscaler_3d_fp16.safetensors through MinimaxH3LatentUpscaler3DRefineHandoff . These are asset references, not bundled weights or proof of architecture, quantization mechanics, license, or GPU compatibility. Resolve matching implementations and assets before queueing. A zero coefficient does not establish that an unavailable LoRA filename will be accepted by every loader or validation system. Read the saved defaults before choosing a route The current export stores main mode ① as true , secondary mode ② as false, refinement ③ as false, preset ④ as 2 , duration ⑥ as 10 seconds , and both manual-LoRA switches ⑦/⑧ as false. The top-level controls route the following inputs: Main mode ① Secondary mode ② Intended route Inputs to replace False False Text-to-video Prompt node 17 False True First/last-frame video Image nodes 97 and 98; prompt 96 True Either Reference-conditioned video Image nodes 26 and 27; prompt 25 The main mode takes precedence through the model, conditioning, and latent switches. In the saved reference configuration, flipping ② alone does not select the first/last-frame route. Each route has its own prompt text. The saved first/last-frame prompt, for example, describes a promotional sequence rather than the same action scene as the reference prompt. Replace the prompt associated with the selected route rather than assuming one global prompt controls all modes. The selected input filenames are not proof that those pictures are included. Supply real, authorized images and inspect which ones reach the active branch. Follow model routing and step selection The ordinary model path starts at loader 2 and passes through the five action-LoRA loaders. The reference path starts at loader 22, adds reference adapter 95, and then passes through its five action-LoRA loaders. Switch 29 selects between those paths using main control 35. Conditioning and latent selectors 30 and 31 follow the same main control. Their ordinary inputs come from the text-versus-first/last selectors 101 and 102; their reference inputs come from node 28. Step selector 108 receives 20 from node 107 on its false branch and 25 from node 33 on its true branch. Its switch input also comes from main control 35. Both scheduler nodes receive this selected step value through links. Consequently, a scheduler's stored 20 widget is not enough to describe the current reference-mode configuration. The sampler selector stores res_multistep . The first scheduler stores simple and denoise 1; the refinement scheduler stores simple and denoise 0.3. The latter value does not establish that refinement executes a full additional 20 or 25 iterations. Actual scheduling and node behavior require the matching implementation and a run record. What the nine automatic presets change Preset node 39 feeds the coefficient expressions. The first-stage manual switch at node 40 determines whether those expressions use their preset recipe or manual values. The second-stage expressions also receive first-stage manual controls and their own override switch at node 68. The following table evaluates the saved expressions with both manual switches false . Values are static arithmetic results, not measured image effects. The order is Combat / Weapon / GunFu / Motion / Fight Flow. Refinement coefficients matter only when that stage is used. Preset label from the source note First-stage coefficients Refinement coefficients A0 Basic action 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 A1 Dynamic-motion repair 1 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0 A2 Two-character interaction 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.65 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.25 A3 Combined action 0.7 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0.65 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0.25 A4 Weapon choreography 0 / 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0 0 / 0.25 / 0 / 0 / 0 A5 GunFu 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0 / 0 A6 Sustained action 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.5 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A7 Close-range action 0.5 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.3 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A8 General motion repair 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.3 / 0 The second-stage recipe is not simply a uniform percentage of the first. A7, for example, has a nonzero first-stage Combat coefficient but zero in its automatic refinement recipe. Enabling either manual switch changes the formula inputs, so the table no longer describes every effective coefficient. Changing the preset number changes these connected coefficient expressions. It does not rewrite the separate prompt strings at nodes 17, 25, or 96. Keep the selected prompt consistent with the fictional scene you intend to generate, and do not assume a preset creates the right action merely because of its label. Duration is a frame budget, not a rendered result Duration node 105 supplies this expression at node 106: max(5, round(a * 24)) + (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17 Its integer output connects to the length inputs of all three generation-condition nodes. Evaluating the expression gives 124 frames for 5 seconds and 243 frames for 10 seconds , both satisfying the intended 17n+5 form. At the configured 24 fps, those budgets correspond arithmetically to approximately 5.17 and 10.13 seconds. They are not measurements of produced video files. The condition nodes' stored length defaults are connected over, so quoting their saved 124 value as the current ten-second setting would be incorrect. Single-stage versus optional refinement With control 59 false, width and height come from resolution selector 104. It stores 16:9, a 0.98-megapixel target, and alignment 32. Those controls describe the selected configuration, not independently checked dimensions. With control 59 true, width and height selectors instead receive 896 and 512 from nodes 60 and 61. Refinement node 65 stores a 1344×768 target , and output switch 66 selects its latent result instead of the first sampler's output. Both video decoder 13 and audio decoder 14 consume that selected latent. The source note warns that the refinement extension may still be required to import or validate the graph even when the refinement switch is off. A disabled route is not a guarantee that missing custom-node classes can be ignored. Use a compatible installation or a separately verified single-stage version; this package does not invent one. Refinement is not guaranteed to improve a particular scene. Compare actual results before describing it as sharper, more faithful, or more stable. Audio and output need their own inspection Reference node 28 has an audio connection from LoadAudio 109, but that loader is saved in mode 4 with a None selection. Verify the installed node's handling of this state instead of assuming that a usable audio reference is present. The graph decodes audio from the selected latent and connects it, alongside decoded video frames, to CreateVideo and then SaveVideo . That is not a direct source-audio remux or proof of synchronized, preserved audio. The save prefix still contains the word Veda , while the current notes say the Turbo/Veda acceleration routes were removed. The node list contains no separately named Turbo/Veda acceleration route. A filename prefix is not evidence that acceleration is active, and this export should not be promoted as an eight-step configuration on that basis. A practical first-run checklist Resolve the exact assets and node implementations, including the optional refinement node's import requirements. Confirm the main route and edit its corresponding prompt. Replace only the relevant image inputs with authorized material. Start with the saved automatic preset controls unless deliberately testing manual weights. Record changes rather than altering several variables at once. Check duration, the selected resolution route, and any audio-reference state before queueing. After an actual run, inspect output dimensions, duration, audio, character consistency, continuity, and whether the intended interaction is visually coherent. No render, compatibility test, performance result, or licensing determination is attached here. The source-provided tutorial offers context; its URL was not live-verified for this package. The local file named as subtitles contains promotional metadata rather than a spoken transcript, so it is not treated as a record of tested behavior. Check workflow, model, LoRA, node, artwork, and input-image rights separately before redistribution or commercial use. Getting the workflow Published by this channel. The graph is free; the weights and LoRAs are separate and carry their own terms. The Bilibili page returned HTTP 412 to this client and was not read.

The useful starting point for this action-video workflow is not its most dramatic promotional claim. It is the control panel: which generation mode is selected, which prompt belongs to that mode, and which LoRA coefficients actually reach the model?

The supplied MiniMax H3 Action Director export is one workflow with 95 nodes and 160 links. Its nine presets are arithmetic recipes inside that graph, not nine independent workflow files. It supports three intended input routes and an optional latent-refinement path. This walkthrough follows the saved configuration; it does not report a new video render, successful character match, or verified action-contact result.

Both base-model loaders select minimax_h3_fl2va_pruned_int8_convrot.safetensors. The reference branch adds minimax_h3_ref_lora_layer20-49adaln_proj_rank_256_bf16.safetensors before its action LoRAs. It does not select a separate Ref2VA checkpoint in this export.

Other common loader references are:

  • qwen3vl_32b_minimax_h3_nvfp4_awq.safetensors, with encoder type minimax;
  • minimax_h3_video_vae_int8_convrot.safetensors;
  • minimax_h3_audio_vae_fp32.safetensors.

The five action-LoRA filenames are H3_Combat_V2.safetensors, Bunny_weapon_combatV1.safetensors, GunFu.safetensors, Motion_Repair_V2.safetensors, and H3_Fight_Flow_V1.safetensors. Optional refinement also references minimax_h3_latent_upscaler_3d_fp16.safetensors through MinimaxH3LatentUpscaler3DRefineHandoff.

These are asset references, not bundled weights or proof of architecture, quantization mechanics, license, or GPU compatibility. Resolve matching implementations and assets before queueing. A zero coefficient does not establish that an unavailable LoRA filename will be accepted by every loader or validation system.

Read the saved defaults before choosing a route

The current export stores main mode ① as true, secondary mode ② as false, refinement ③ as false, preset ④ as 2, duration ⑥ as 10 seconds, and both manual-LoRA switches ⑦/⑧ as false.

The top-level controls route the following inputs:

Main mode ① Secondary mode ② Intended route Inputs to replace False False Text-to-video Prompt node 17 False True First/last-frame video Image nodes 97 and 98; prompt 96 True Either Reference-conditioned video Image nodes 26 and 27; prompt 25

The main mode takes precedence through the model, conditioning, and latent switches. In the saved reference configuration, flipping ② alone does not select the first/last-frame route.

Each route has its own prompt text. The saved first/last-frame prompt, for example, describes a promotional sequence rather than the same action scene as the reference prompt. Replace the prompt associated with the selected route rather than assuming one global prompt controls all modes.

The selected input filenames are not proof that those pictures are included. Supply real, authorized images and inspect which ones reach the active branch.

Follow model routing and step selection

The ordinary model path starts at loader 2 and passes through the five action-LoRA loaders. The reference path starts at loader 22, adds reference adapter 95, and then passes through its five action-LoRA loaders. Switch 29 selects between those paths using main control 35.

Conditioning and latent selectors 30 and 31 follow the same main control. Their ordinary inputs come from the text-versus-first/last selectors 101 and 102; their reference inputs come from node 28.

Step selector 108 receives 20 from node 107 on its false branch and 25 from node 33 on its true branch. Its switch input also comes from main control 35. Both scheduler nodes receive this selected step value through links. Consequently, a scheduler's stored 20 widget is not enough to describe the current reference-mode configuration.

The sampler selector stores res_multistep. The first scheduler stores simple and denoise 1; the refinement scheduler stores simple and denoise 0.3. The latter value does not establish that refinement executes a full additional 20 or 25 iterations. Actual scheduling and node behavior require the matching implementation and a run record.

What the nine automatic presets change

Preset node 39 feeds the coefficient expressions. The first-stage manual switch at node 40 determines whether those expressions use their preset recipe or manual values. The second-stage expressions also receive first-stage manual controls and their own override switch at node 68.

The following table evaluates the saved expressions with both manual switches false. Values are static arithmetic results, not measured image effects. The order is Combat / Weapon / GunFu / Motion / Fight Flow. Refinement coefficients matter only when that stage is used.

Preset label from the source note First-stage coefficients Refinement coefficients A0 Basic action 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0 A1 Dynamic-motion repair 1 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0 A2 Two-character interaction 0.65 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.65 0.4 / 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.25 A3 Combined action 0.7 / 0 / 0 / 0.5 / 0.65 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0.2 / 0.25 A4 Weapon choreography 0 / 0.45 / 0 / 0 / 0 0 / 0.25 / 0 / 0 / 0 A5 GunFu 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0 / 0 A6 Sustained action 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.5 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A7 Close-range action 0.5 / 0 / 0.9 / 0.3 / 0 0 / 0 / 0.65 / 0.25 / 0 A8 General motion repair 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.9 / 0 0 / 0 / 0 / 0.3 / 0

The second-stage recipe is not simply a uniform percentage of the first. A7, for example, has a nonzero first-stage Combat coefficient but zero in its automatic refinement recipe. Enabling either manual switch changes the formula inputs, so the table no longer describes every effective coefficient.

Changing the preset number changes these connected coefficient expressions. It does not rewrite the separate prompt strings at nodes 17, 25, or 96. Keep the selected prompt consistent with the fictional scene you intend to generate, and do not assume a preset creates the right action merely because of its label.

Duration is a frame budget, not a rendered result

Duration node 105 supplies this expression at node 106:

max(5, round(a * 24)) + (5 - (max(5, round(a * 24)) % 17)) % 17

Its integer output connects to the length inputs of all three generation-condition nodes. Evaluating the expression gives 124 frames for 5 seconds and 243 frames for 10 seconds, both satisfying the intended 17n+5 form.

At the configured 24 fps, those budgets correspond arithmetically to approximately 5.17 and 10.13 seconds. They are not measurements of produced video files. The condition nodes' stored length defaults are connected over, so quoting their saved 124 value as the current ten-second setting would be incorrect.

Single-stage versus optional refinement

With control 59 false, width and height come from resolution selector 104. It stores 16:9, a 0.98-megapixel target, and alignment 32. Those controls describe the selected configuration, not independently checked dimensions.

With control 59 true, width and height selectors instead receive 896 and 512 from nodes 60 and 61. Refinement node 65 stores a 1344×768 target, and output switch 66 selects its latent result instead of the first sampler's output. Both video decoder 13 and audio decoder 14 consume that selected latent.

The source note warns that the refinement extension may still be required to import or validate the graph even when the refinement switch is off. A disabled route is not a guarantee that missing custom-node classes can be ignored. Use a compatible installation or a separately verified single-stage version; this package does not invent one.

Refinement is not guaranteed to improve a particular scene. Compare actual results before describing it as sharper, more faithful, or more stable.

Audio and output need their own inspection

Reference node 28 has an audio connection from LoadAudio 109, but that loader is saved in mode 4 with a None selection. Verify the installed node's handling of this state instead of assuming that a usable audio reference is present.

The graph decodes audio from the selected latent and connects it, alongside decoded video frames, to CreateVideo and then SaveVideo. That is not a direct source-audio remux or proof of synchronized, preserved audio.

The save prefix still contains the word Veda, while the current notes say the Turbo/Veda acceleration routes were removed. The node list contains no separately named Turbo/Veda acceleration route. A filename prefix is not evidence that acceleration is active, and this export should not be promoted as an eight-step configuration on that basis.

A practical first-run checklist
  1. Resolve the exact assets and node implementations, including the optional refinement node's import requirements.
  2. Confirm the main route and edit its corresponding prompt. Replace only the relevant image inputs with authorized material.
  3. Start with the saved automatic preset controls unless deliberately testing manual weights. Record changes rather than altering several variables at once.
  4. Check duration, the selected resolution route, and any audio-reference state before queueing.
  5. After an actual run, inspect output dimensions, duration, audio, character consistency, continuity, and whether the intended interaction is visually coherent.

No render, compatibility test, performance result, or licensing determination is attached here. The source-provided tutorial offers context; its URL was not live-verified for this package. summary_html:
Originally published on the Kulissa blog: Why sales reps forget most of their training, and what actually sticks

Sales enablement loves a packed agenda. Product decks. Competitive slides. Role-play that lasts until someone looks at the clock. Then Monday arrives, the calendar fills, and the classroom becomes a blur.

ATD's State of Sales Training 2023, citing Gartner, reports that B2B reps forget about 70% of training within a week and 87% within a month unless they use it. First-year sellers still spend more than ten days in formal training. That is a lot of stage time that never makes it into the show.

The forgetting curve is not a mystery. Hermann Ebbinghaus mapped it more than a century ago: unused memory decays fast, then slower. What surprises revenue leaders is how often the curriculum assumes the opposite. We treat exposure as competence. We treat a single rehearsal as muscle memory. The call, of course, is the reveal. Without practice under pressure, the wings stay crowded and the performance stays thin.

The classroom was never the stage

Formal training is useful for shared language. It is a poor substitute for live conversation. A workshop can introduce a discovery framework. It cannot teach a rep what to do when a buyer cuts them off mid-sentence, or when procurement joins on minute twelve with a price objection the playbook never covered in that order.

Most programs optimize for coverage. Cover the ICP. Cover the competitors. Cover the objection list. Coverage feels responsible. It also creates a false sense of readiness. The Bridge Group's AE Models, Motions and Metrics 2026 puts average AE ramp at 6.2 months, with only 48% of AEs at quota. If classroom hours alone closed the gap, those numbers would look different.

Reps do not forget because they are lazy. They forget because the brain prioritizes what gets retrieved under load. A slide deck is passive. A live buyer is not. Without retrieval practice, the methodology stays in the binder.

Three reasons training evaporates 1. Spacing is optional, not designed

Enablement often runs as an event. Kickoff week. Quarterly SKO. A two-day bootcamp for new hires. Dense input, thin follow-up. Spaced retrieval is what keeps skills available. Without it, the first week of forgetting does the predictable damage.

A practical rule: if a skill matters on the phone, schedule at least three short practice reps across ten days after the workshop. Not another lecture. Practice.

2. Feedback arrives late or not at all

Managers coach when they have time. Call recordings help, but they coach after the fact. The rep already shipped the performance. Delayed feedback still helps for pattern recognition. It does less for building automatic responses under interruption.

Ericsson's research on deliberate practice is blunt about this. Improvement needs a clear goal, immediate feedback, and repetition at the edge of current ability. Most sales "practice" fails two of the three: goals are vague ("be more consultative"), feedback is sparse, and the difficulty never climbs.

3. The scoreboard rewards activity, not readiness

Pipeline reviews count meetings and stage movement. Training completion is a checkbox. Neither tells you whether a rep can hold a value conversation when the buyer is cold. When the org measures attendance, people attend. When it measures live performance against a shared scorecard, people rehearse.

What actually sticks

Skills stick when three conditions hold.

Retrieval under pressure. The rep must produce the behavior without a slide behind them. Voice practice with interruptions beats watching a model call.

Evidence-based coaching. Vague praise ("good energy") does not change behavior. Quoted transcript moments do. "You skipped the impact question after they said budget was frozen" is actionable.

Playbook-native scenarios. Generic AI buyers teach generic habits. Scenarios built from your own discovery framework, objection tree, and competitive traps teach the show your team actually runs. That is the difference between theatre games and dress rehearsal.

If you want a Monday-ready test for any training module, ask:

  1. Can the rep demonstrate the skill live in under five minutes?
  2. Is there a shared rubric that names pass and fail behaviors?
  3. Will they practice again within 72 hours with a harder version?

If any answer is no, you bought exposure, not readiness.

A simple retention design for enablement

Use this as a template for the next cohort, not as a manifesto.

  • 0. Input: 45-minute workshop on one skill; Practice: None; Check: Pre-assessment score
  • 1. Input: Short reminder card; Practice: One 8-minute scenario; Check: Rubric score + one coach note
  • 3. Input: Peer listen-in (optional); Practice: Harder buyer temperature; Check: Rubric delta vs day 1
  • 7. Input: None; Practice: Same skill, new persona; Check: Pass threshold or rematch
  • 14. Input: Manager 1:1 on evidence; Practice: Assignment based on weak dimension; Check: Cohort readiness view

Keep the curriculum narrow. One skill per cycle beats five half-learned skills. The sales onboarding plan for the first 30 days expands this into a full ramp calendar. For teams rebuilding from methodology documents, turning a playbook into roleplay scenarios is the conversion step most enablement skips.

Where conversation intelligence fits (and where it does not)

Gong-style conversation intelligence is excellent for coaching real calls. It is a poor primary practice loop. You cannot schedule enough live buyer meetings to create deliberate practice volume. You also cannot ask a strategic account to be your classroom.

Role-play and conversation intelligence are complementary. Practice builds the skill. Recorded calls audit transfer to the field. Treating recordings as the only gym is like only reviewing game film and never running drills. The longer comparison is in role-play vs conversation intelligence.

How this works in Kulissa

Kulissa is built around rehearsal before the reveal. A rep opens the browser, speaks into the microphone, and faces a live AI buyer who interrupts, objects, and changes temperature. Sessions are transcribed and scored against your methodology, with evidence quoted from the transcript. Scenarios can be generated from your playbooks so practice stays native to how you sell.

Managers see readiness by rep and cohort, not just completion. That matters if your goal is retention of skill, not attendance. Product detail lives on kulissa.com/product. If ramp and onboarding are the pain, start with kulissa.com/use-cases/sales-onboarding.

Maya on kulissa.com/maya is the public gatekeeper demo: convince her your team deserves access, and you can win promotional credits for a workspace. It is a rehearsal of the product idea itself.

The uncomfortable conclusion

If 87% of unused training fades within a month, the expensive part of enablement is not the facilitator. It is the false confidence. Teams that treat practice as a first-class operating system reduce that waste. Teams that keep buying more slides keep buying forgetting.

The stage does not care how many workshops you attended. It cares whether the line lands when someone talks over you.

What enablement leaders should stop funding

Before you renew another content library, ask whether last year's modules produced measurable retrieval. If the only dashboard is completion percentage, you are funding forgetting with better production value.

Stop funding:

  • One-time certifications with no rematch window
  • Manager "coaching" that is really forecast interrogation
  • Competitive battle cards that are never practiced aloud
  • Kickoff theatre that crowds out the first two weeks of spaced practice

Start funding:

  • Scenario libraries tied to loss reasons
  • Manager calibration time on shared scorecards
  • Protected practice blocks on the AE calendar
  • Rematch capacity when someone fails a gate

This is capital allocation, not pedagogy fashion. The forgetting curve does not care about your brand fonts.

A worked example: discovery that does not stick

Imagine a two-day onboarding that covers discovery thoroughly. Reps can recite the question list. On day ten, a buyer asks for pricing in minute two. Most reps pitch. The discovery list was never retrieved under interruption, so it never became available.

Now change the design. After the workshop, every rep runs three scenarios: friendly discovery, price-interrupt discovery, and dual-stakeholder discovery. Failures rematch within forty-eight hours. Managers quote transcript lines in 1:1s. By day fourteen, the question list is no longer a list. It is a reflex with judgment.

Same content hours. Different retention. The difference is deliberate retrieval, which is also why deliberate practice for sales teams belongs next to this article on your enablement reading list.

Measuring retention without fake precision

You do not need a neuroscience lab. You need three operational signals:

  1. Scenario rematch rate falling over a cohort's first month
  2. Dimension stability when the same skill is tested ten days later with a new persona
  3. Live transfer on conversation intelligence reviews using the same rubric language

If signal one improves while signal three stays flat, your scenarios are too polite. If signal two collapses, you never had learning; you had short-term performance. If all three move, congratulations: you built a practice system instead of a content museum.

Sources
  • ATD, State of Sales Training 2023 (citing Gartner on training forgetting rates and first-year formal training days)
  • The Bridge Group, AE Models, Motions and Metrics 2026 (AE ramp and quota attainment)
  • Ericsson, K. Anders et al., research on deliberate practice and expert performance
  • Ebbinghaus, Hermann, work on the forgetting curve (classic memory research)
FAQ Why do sales reps forget training so quickly?

Because unused memory decays fast, and most programs deliver dense input without scheduled retrieval under pressure. ATD citing Gartner puts forgetting near 70% within a week and 87% within a month unless the material is used. Classroom coverage without live practice accelerates that curve.

How many practice sessions does it take for a skill to stick?

There is no universal magic number, but spaced practice with feedback beats one marathon. A workable pattern is three to five short scenarios across two weeks for a single skill, each scored against a shared rubric, with difficulty rising as the rep clears the bar.

Does conversation intelligence replace practice?

No. Conversation intelligence coaches real calls after they happen. Deliberate practice needs volume, controlled difficulty, and immediate feedback. Recordings and role-play work best together: drills for building skill, film for transferring it to live deals.

What should managers measure instead of training completion?

Measure demonstrated readiness: rubric scores on live practice, weak dimensions by cohort, and rematch rates after a failed scenario. Completion proves attendance. Scored rehearsal proves whether the skill is available on stage.

  • Role-play vs conversation intelligence: which one builds the skill
  • A sales onboarding plan for the first 30 days that puts practice before pipeline

title: Anthropic's internal AI use, valued at retail prices, now exceeds its employee pay
summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Aaron Schwartz/Bloomberg via Getty Images A version of this story originally appeared in the AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly AI Insider newsletter here . Here's a remarkable milestone in the AI revolution: Anthropic now spends more on internal AI usage than it does paying employees. The company revealed this in its IPO filing . In April, the value of Claude AI used internally, calculated at prices Anthropic charges customers, exceeded its monthly employee compensation costs, excluding stock awards. By September, that internal AI usage had surged more than 250-fold since January. There's an important distinction here. Anthropic isn't actually spending more cash on AI than salaries. It's valuing its internal AI consumption at retail prices. Still, this feels like a watershed moment for the tech industry. In March, I wrote about a new trend : Tech companies are starting to treat AI tokens (the main way to measure usage) as a fourth component of employee compensation, alongside salary, bonuses, and stock awards. Anthropic's numbers show why. More than 90% of the code added to its software in September was written by Claude. Meanwhile, revenue has grown vastly faster than headcount. For decades, talented humans were the most valuable resource in Silicon Valley. Now AI is challenging that assumption. Sign up for the AI Insider newsletter here . Reach out to me via email at abarr@businessinsider.com Read the original article on Business Insider
