title: A step-by-step guide for how to kill the line-by-line code review
summary: Agents verify; people decide. Most teams running AI code review today have it the other way around. They point a model at the diff, ask it whether the change is good, and leave a human to skim the result and click approve. The model reads every line, never gets tired, and holds the same standard on every PR. What it doesn’t have is your codebase’s standards. It doesn’t know them, and no matter how well you instruct it, it doesn’t always follow the ones you write down. “Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person.” It never saw what was decided, has no context for previous decisions, can’t tell you not to build the thing, and can’t be held accountable. A diff can’t give it any of that. Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person. So what does a code review look like when verification goes to agents and judgment stays with people? At Aviator, we’ve been building that review into Aviator Verify . Below are its seven parts, in order. The anatomy of an intent-driven review Click to enlarge image. Every change gets checked against two layers . Acceptance criteria describe what this change should do. Invariants are the codified rules of your engineering org or team: the standards that are always true, whatever the change. Criteria without invariants leave your standards to memory. Every engineer has to remember every standard, or someone has to catch the obvious agent mistakes in code review. Invariants without criteria give you code that follows the rules but doesn’t consider what the result should be, so the agent strays, overengineers, or solves the wrong problem. The seven parts build both layers, verify the change against them, and hand the decision to a person: Invariants (defined before any change): the team’s standing rules, drawn from its own code reviews. Intent and acceptance criteria (captured from the coding session): why the change exists and how it should behave. Core decisions (captured from the coding session): the choices made along the way, and who made them. A test plan (built at submit): the criteria plus the invariants that apply, turned into scenarios. Evidence (gathered at submit): proof from a running environment behind every verdict. A review (decided by a person): intent, decisions, and evidence, approved or pushed back on. Not code. Invariants refreshed (updated after merge): waivers and recurring comments that sharpen the invariants. 1. Invariants Every review checks a change against something. In most teams, that something lives in senior engineers’ heads and comes out as review comments. Use the Money type for anything with a currency. No direct writes to the users table. Every error path emits a counter. Each of those has been typed more than once, and coding agents keep making the same mistakes because the rule was never written down anywhere an agent or a verifier could use it. An invariant is that rule, written once and checked on every matching change. Together, your invariants become an AI slop registry , the running list of patterns your team keeps correcting. Agent instruction files like CLAUDE.md help, but they’re an input to generation. The same non-deterministic agent that wrote the code is asked to follow them, and nothing proves it did. Invariants sit on the verification side, checked by a deterministic script or at least a different agent that returns a verdict for each rule. Your PR history already holds most of them. Verify reads the comments your team posts in GitHub and drafts invariants from the patterns it finds. It also drafts them from CONTRIBUTING.md and agent instruction files or on the spot when someone tags @aviator invariant in a PR comment or a Slack thread. Generate your team’s invariants with the Aviator Verify free account and keep them even if you decide not to continue with Verify. Three things determine whether an invariant helps or becomes noise. Ownership. Every draft goes to the team it belongs to, with the reason it was proposed, and goes live only once that team approves it. Nothing AI-drafted becomes a standing check without a human saying yes. Wording. Assert the outcome and leave the implementation open, so the rule survives renames and file moves. Scope. A rule should only run where it can break. A frontend invariant has no business checking database migrations. 2. Intent and acceptance criteria The obvious way to give a reviewer intent is to write a spec up front or capture as a detailed JIRA ticket. Specs take time, get written before the work teaches anyone anything, and drift the moment implementation starts. The most accurate intent already exists in the coding session. Every time the agent stops to ask a question and the engineer makes a call, acceptance criteria get defined in real time. There is no reason to throw all of that away when the session ends! The intent says why the change was made. The acceptance criteria say how it should behave. Verify captures both from the session the engineer already had. An agent skill and a hook run verify submit before the agent opens a pull request. The agent extracts the intent and the criteria from everything it saw in the session, and the engineer reviews and corrects them before anything is submitted. Click to enlarge image. 3. Core decisions A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way. Where state lives, what happens when a dependency fails, whether to reuse an existing helper or write a new one. An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff. “An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff.” Verify records the decisions next to the intent, with humans and agents labeled separately, so the reviewer knows who made which call and can argue with it. I wrote more about why decisions are the thing people should review in How to review AI code without reading the code . 4. A test plan When a change is submitted, Verify reads the intent and the criteria and uses the diff to identify the invariants to apply. Both layers merge into one list of scenarios: the steps an agent takes to validate behavior, derived from the requirements rather than the code. That’s where the two layers pay off. The engineer stays focused on the change, and the registry covers the standards. 5. Evidence When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots. Verification must be structurally separate from generation, and it must produce more than an opinion. “When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots.” Verify spins up a preview environment and dispatches verifier agents to run the scenarios. They capture screenshots, database state, server logs, and console logs, and every verdict, for a criterion or an invariant, points at that evidence. For a UI change, the verifier actually clicks through the interface and confirms the result. You don’t need a preview on day one. Code scans handle structural checks straight from the diff, with no infrastructure, and many invariants are converted to deterministic scripts. A preview earns its place once your criteria start asking about behavior the diff can’t show. 6. A review This is where people come back in, and the work looks different. As a reviewer, you’re looking at evidence rather than reading code line by line. You read the intent, look at the hot spots where the core changes are, go through the decisions and the verdict on each criterion and invariant, and open the live preview if you want to see the change for yourself. Click to enlarge image. The pull request workflow barely changes. Verify adds a link to the review, the diff stays where it was, and the results are reported as a status check similar to the CI behavior. The reviewer answers one question: does the evidence match what the team agreed to build? They approve, push back on a decision, ask for another scenario, or waive a failed invariant with a reason. That’s judgment, and someone owns it. 7. Invariants refreshed Most reviews end at merge, and everything they learned leaves with them. The next PR makes the same mistake, and the same comment shows up again. Invariants keep what each review learned. When an invariant fails on a PR, the author can waive it with a reason: maybe it doesn’t apply, maybe the invariant is incorrect, or maybe it gets fixed separately. The team that owns the Invariants sees every waiver. Click to enlarge image. Insights show which invariants apply most, how often each one fails, and why people waive them. An invariant that keeps getting waived is wrong, so the team rewrites or narrows it. A comment reviewers keep typing becomes the next draft. Agents verify; people decide. Most teams running AI code review today have it the other way around. They point a model at the diff, ask it whether the change is good, and leave a human to skim the result and click approve.

The model reads every line, never gets tired, and holds the same standard on every PR. What it doesn’t have is your codebase’s standards. It doesn’t know them, and no matter how well you instruct it, it doesn’t always follow the ones you write down.

“Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person.”

It never saw what was decided, has no context for previous decisions, can’t tell you not to build the thing, and can’t be held accountable. A diff can’t give it any of that. Judgment needs intent, and accountability needs a person.

So what does a code review look like when verification goes to agents and judgment stays with people? At Aviator, we’ve been building that review into Aviator Verify. Below are its seven parts, in order.

The anatomy of an intent-driven review Click to enlarge image.

Every change gets checked against two layers. Acceptance criteria describe what this change should do. Invariants are the codified rules of your engineering org or team: the standards that are always true, whatever the change. 

Criteria without invariants leave your standards to memory. Every engineer has to remember every standard, or someone has to catch the obvious agent mistakes in code review. Invariants without criteria give you code that follows the rules but doesn’t consider what the result should be, so the agent strays, overengineers, or solves the wrong problem.

The seven parts build both layers, verify the change against them, and hand the decision to a person:

  1. Invariants (defined before any change): the team’s standing rules, drawn from its own code reviews.
  2. Intent and acceptance criteria (captured from the coding session): why the change exists and how it should behave.
  3. Core decisions (captured from the coding session): the choices made along the way, and who made them.
  4. A test plan (built at submit): the criteria plus the invariants that apply, turned into scenarios.
  5. Evidence (gathered at submit): proof from a running environment behind every verdict.
  6. A review (decided by a person): intent, decisions, and evidence, approved or pushed back on. Not code.
  7. Invariants refreshed (updated after merge): waivers and recurring comments that sharpen the invariants.
1. Invariants

Every review checks a change against something. In most teams, that something lives in senior engineers’ heads and comes out as review comments. Use the Money type for anything with a currency. No direct writes to the users table. Every error path emits a counter. Each of those has been typed more than once, and coding agents keep making the same mistakes because the rule was never written down anywhere an agent or a verifier could use it.

An invariant is that rule, written once and checked on every matching change. Together, your invariants become an AI slop registry, the running list of patterns your team keeps correcting.

Agent instruction files like CLAUDE.md help, but they’re an input to generation. The same non-deterministic agent that wrote the code is asked to follow them, and nothing proves it did. Invariants sit on the verification side, checked by a deterministic script or at least a different agent that returns a verdict for each rule. 

Your PR history already holds most of them. Verify reads the comments your team posts in GitHub and drafts invariants from the patterns it finds. It also drafts them from CONTRIBUTING.md and agent instruction files or on the spot when someone tags @aviator invariant in a PR comment or a Slack thread. Generate your team’s invariants with the Aviator Verify free account and keep them even if you decide not to continue with Verify.

Three things determine whether an invariant helps or becomes noise.

  • Ownership. Every draft goes to the team it belongs to, with the reason it was proposed, and goes live only once that team approves it. Nothing AI-drafted becomes a standing check without a human saying yes.
  • Wording. Assert the outcome and leave the implementation open, so the rule survives renames and file moves.
  • Scope. A rule should only run where it can break. A frontend invariant has no business checking database migrations.
2. Intent and acceptance criteria

The obvious way to give a reviewer intent is to write a spec up front or capture as a detailed JIRA ticket. Specs take time, get written before the work teaches anyone anything, and drift the moment implementation starts.

The most accurate intent already exists in the coding session. Every time the agent stops to ask a question and the engineer makes a call, acceptance criteria get defined in real time. There is no reason to throw all of that away when the session ends!

The intent says why the change was made. The acceptance criteria say how it should behave. 

Verify captures both from the session the engineer already had. An agent skill and a hook run verify submit before the agent opens a pull request. The agent extracts the intent and the criteria from everything it saw in the session, and the engineer reviews and corrects them before anything is submitted.

Click to enlarge image. 3. Core decisions

A decision is any point where the change could have gone another way. Where state lives, what happens when a dependency fails, whether to reuse an existing helper or write a new one. An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff.

“An AI-written PR is full of calls like these, and almost none of them show up in the diff.”

Verify records the decisions next to the intent, with humans and agents labeled separately, so the reviewer knows who made which call and can argue with it. I wrote more about why decisions are the thing people should review in How to review AI code without reading the code.

4. A test plan

When a change is submitted, Verify reads the intent and the criteria and uses the diff to identify the invariants to apply. Both layers merge into one list of scenarios: the steps an agent takes to validate behavior, derived from the requirements rather than the code.

That’s where the two layers pay off. The engineer stays focused on the change, and the registry covers the standards.

5. Evidence

When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots. Verification must be structurally separate from generation, and it must produce more than an opinion.

“When the same model writes and reviews the code, they share the same blind spots.”

Verify spins up a preview environment and dispatches verifier agents to run the scenarios. They capture screenshots, database state, server logs, and console logs, and every verdict, for a criterion or an invariant, points at that evidence. For a UI change, the verifier actually clicks through the interface and confirms the result.

You don’t need a preview on day one. Code scans handle structural checks straight from the diff, with no infrastructure, and many invariants are converted to deterministic scripts. A preview earns its place once your criteria start asking about behavior the diff can’t show.

6. A review

This is where people come back in, and the work looks different. As a reviewer, you’re looking at evidence rather than reading code line by line. You read the intent, look at the hot spots where the core changes are, go through the decisions and the verdict on each criterion and invariant, and open the live preview if you want to see the change for yourself.

Click to enlarge image.

The pull request workflow barely changes. Verify adds a link to the review, the diff stays where it was, and the results are reported as a status check similar to the CI behavior.

The reviewer answers one question: does the evidence match what the team agreed to build? They approve, push back on a decision, ask for another scenario, or waive a failed invariant with a reason. That’s judgment, and someone owns it.

7. Invariants refreshed

Most reviews end at merge, and everything they learned leaves with them. The next PR makes the same mistake, and the same comment shows up again.

Invariants keep what each review learned. When an invariant fails on a PR, the author can waive it with a reason: maybe it doesn’t apply, maybe the invariant is incorrect, or maybe it gets fixed separately. The team that owns the Invariants sees every waiver.

title: Trump Living in Alternate World of AI Slop, Insiders Say
summary: President Donald Trump’s obsession with AI is even grimmer than we believed. The commander-in-chief has hardly hidden his enchantment with AI slop, regularly posting bizarre AI videos glorifying himself, denigrating his foes, and at times, attempting to rewrite reality . But a behind-the-scenes look suggests that Trump is now completely lost in an AI alternate reality of his own making. While Republicans scramble and prepare for what could be a disastrous midterm election season for their party, sources told the New York Times that Trump is cloistering himself in a world made of sycophantic press coverage, disparaging clips about his foes, and, not least of all, “AI slop,” in the words of one White House official. One person keeping him hooked on the stuff is Bill Pulte, a top federal housing official. According to the reporting, Pulte regularly joins Trump in his cabin on Air Force One and shows him memes — some of which are almost certainly AI-generated — posters, and documents related to the mortgage industry. One administration official even described Pulte as a “court jester.” Trump is now so isolated from critical coverage that his indignation and incredulity when encountering it can be petulant and extreme. When comedian Bill Maher — who you wouldn’t describe as particularly left wing — joked about Trump’s ties to Jeffrey Epstein and his affinity for Russia, Trump’s response was absurdly disproportionate: a maniacal 1,300 word rant raging against Maher that he posted on his website Truth Social, which breaking news accounts on social media struggled to capture in one screenshot . The signs of his AI infirmity have long been apparent. But some worry that AI is playing a direct role in the president’s decision-making, too. A recent scoop from TIME magazine reported that Trump is so enthralled by Elon Musk’s chatbot Grok that his conversations with it encouraged him to invade Venezuela and capture its president Nicolas Maduro. Top Democrats are now demanding to see those Grok conversations and others . title: Cisco Gives a Former Startup Founder an AI Budget With No Ceiling
summary: Cisco’s Unlimited-Token Refactor Shifts the Bottleneck From Writing Code to Proving It Cisco president Jeetu Patel has given one engineer unlimited AI tokens and 24 months to refactor 98% of the company’s legacy code. The cost ceiling that normally stops a project of this size is gone, which leaves a harder question: how Cisco will prove the refactored code still behaves like the original. A Four-Week Proof of Concept Comes First Patel described the plan to Fortune at a small roundtable dinner, and the outlet published the account on October 30, 2026. The engineer is Padmanabhan “Paddy” Krishnamurthy, 27, who cofounded the real-time translation startup EzDubs in 2023 and joined Cisco when it acquired the company in 2025. Patel told Fortune he found Krishnamurthy five levels below him in the organization, working on something Patel called unstrategic. Krishnamurthy told Patel he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a team of two, and Patel said even the most AI-forward people on his own team were not thinking that way. A four-week proof of concept comes first, with the 98% target due within 24 months. On tokens, Patel’s instruction was to “go nuts.” Fortune’s report does not say which products or how many lines of code count as legacy, and it carries no results from the proof of concept. The coverage uses “refactor” and “rewrite” interchangeably, and they are not the same job. Refactoring restructures code while keeping its behavior identical; a rewrite can change what the software does. Patel’s own word was refactor, which sets the stricter standard: whatever the AI produces has to act exactly like what it replaced. Generation Gets Cheap, Verification Does Not Earlier large migrations show where the effort goes once generation costs little. Airbnb moved nearly 3,500 React test files from Enzyme to React Testing Library in about six weeks, against a manual estimate of 1.5 years. Its pipeline ran each file through automated Jest, lint and TypeScript checks and retried failures up to a set limit. A first bulk run reached 75% of files in four hours, and four days of prompt and script refinement lifted completion to 97%. Engineers fixed the remaining 100 or so files by hand, which took about another week. Google reported a similar pattern in a paper on its internal migrations. In an int32-to-int64 ID change across the Google Ads codebase, which spans more than 500 million lines, AI wrote 80% of the code modifications in landed changes, and engineers estimated a 50% cut in total time. The authors also reported that in most cases the engineer had to revert at least some of the model’s changes, and they named the speed of human review as the bottleneck. GitHub’s numbers show where that load lands. The platform recorded 7.38 billion commits in September 2026, more than five times the figure a year earlier, and GitHub Actions, its workflow automation service, ran 3.26 billion times, more than four times as often as a year before. The implication is that every company letting agents write code at that pace inherits the same multiplier on its own build and test systems. Cisco Has Already Named the Standard In an interview with SDxCentral, Patel said organizations should prepare for a world in which humans cannot review all the code AI writes, and that teams must “automate the test beds and harnesses” that measure outputs. He added that whoever evaluates those outputs should answer for the code, and that every piece of it should trace back to a human. In the same interview he said Cisco’s AI Defense product was built entirely with AI, and he set targets of about half a dozen fully AI-written products by the end of 2026 and roughly 70% of the portfolio by the end of 2027. Those are targets, not results. One way to read the legacy refactor is as the older-code counterpart to that strategy, facing the same test. The implication is that Cisco’s test coverage, more than its token spend, will decide whether the 98% figure holds. Fortune’s report does not say how Cisco will measure it, and the four-week proof of concept is the first chance to show a method exists. What to Have in Place Before You Try This Fortune’s report does not describe Cisco’s method, so what follows is advice drawn from the Airbnb and Google cases and from Patel’s stated standard, not a description of what Cisco does. If you plan a large AI-driven refactor, settle three things before you spend the first token. Test coverage that can fail the code. Airbnb’s pipeline worked because every migrated file faced an automatic judge: it passed the Jest, lint and TypeScript checks or it went back for another attempt. Production code needs the same kind of referee. Map which of the modules you plan to change have tests that would catch a behavior change, and write tests that record what the code does today for the ones that do not. Do that before the model touches them, because a test written against the model’s output can only confirm what the model already did. A named owner for every change. Patel’s stated standard is that whoever evaluates AI output should answer for the code, and that every piece of it should trace to a human. Google’s paper found that engineers reverted at least some of the model’s changes in most cases, so someone has to read each diff and sign for it. Assign owners by module before the run starts. Then budget their review hours as a line item, since Google named the speed of human review as the bottleneck. A pass-rate threshold fixed in advance. Decide before the first run what share of changes must pass your checks unchanged for the project to continue, and what happens to the rest. Airbnb’s first bulk run cleared 75% of files in four hours, four days of tuning lifted completion to 97%, and the final 100 or so files took about another week by hand. The long tail is where the schedule goes, so staff for it. The right number depends on what a failure costs in that system: a test-file migration can tolerate more misses than a payments service. Cisco’s four-week proof of concept is where these three items will show up first. If Cisco discloses how much of the refactored code passed its existing tests unchanged and how many reviewer hours the rest consumed, the industry gets rare evidence from a company that builds networking infrastructure. Without those numbers, the 98% target stays an ambition with an open-ended token allowance behind it.

title: A 'humbling' career move led to Catherine Zeta-Jones' big break
summary: Catherine Zeta-Jones currently stars in "Killing Jackie." Getty; TriStar Pictures; USA Films; BI Catherine Zeta-Jones' arrival in Hollywood in the mid-1990s was an ego check. The Welsh actor, then in her 20s, had starred for years on the popular early-'90s British series "The Darling Buds of May," and was already a sensation in the UK. But when she touched down in California, she went from being recognized on the street to having casting agents ask her in auditions if she had any acting experience. That wasn't all. "I couldn't get cable TV," Zeta-Jones told Business Insider with a laugh. "I had been working since I was 9, but I couldn't buy anything in the States because I didn't have a credit card yet. I had to start from scratch." Starting over turned out to be worth it for Zeta-Jones. After taking a role in the CBS miniseries "Titanic," she caught the attention of Steven Spielberg , who recommended her for "The Mask of Zorro." The role would make her a star Stateside and lead to an illustrious three-decade career in Hollywood. title: Innocent People Are Being Accused of Shoplifting by Faulty AI-Facial Recognition Systems at an Alarming Rate
summary: From New York City to the streets of Tokyo , creepy AI-facial recognition security systems are quickly becoming a common sight across the world. Unfortunately for many, the tech is nowhere near ready for the responsibility of live use as the troubling rise of false-positive matches makes clear. In the United Kingdom, AI surveillance systems in retail stores have led to a surge in customers being wrongly accused of shoplifting. TechRadar highlighted a number of recent cases throughout the country, where shoppers say false accusations have left them shaken, with a feeling that their privacy had been horribly violated. As one woman identified as Mary told the publication, her husband has been socially “isolated” after a quick jaunt into a Home Bargains store for vitamins went awry. When the stores’ system flagged the anonymous man as a shoplifter, the couple was forced to leave by management, seemingly without any chance to refute the accusation. “I was scared to go into a shop,” the man told TechRadar . Another man was said to be “shaking from head to toe” following his wife’s removal from a Budgens chain store for the crime of stealing “loads of meat” days before — an accusation complicated by the fact that they hadn’t set foot in the store for months. In these and other cases, the publication reports a dizzying labyrinth of corporate bureaucracy and vague insinuations that leave innocent people unable to access their local businesses, and with little recourse to clear their name. In the UK, individuals can file Subject Access Requests, or SARs, which are like US-Freedom of Information Act requests but for private companies. Though the avenue technically exists for those wrongly accused of shoplifting, it’s a massive undertaking just for the hope of clearing your name — and requires handing over even more private information to private companies. As head of advocacy at civil liberty group Big Brother Watch Jack Coulson told TechRadar , it’s “the stuff of Kafkaesque nightmares to be trapped in a maze of bureaucracy and forced to hand over even more personal data just to be told the accusation.” More on facial recognition: Innocent Man Freed After Spending Over 50 Days in Jail Due to Horribly Inaccurate AI Facial Recognition Tech

title: Fox News Takes Massive Ratings Hit As It Triples Down on Pro-Data Center Coverage
summary: It’s obvious by now that data centers are political kryptonite. Across the US, bipartisan backlash to data center projects has upended city councils , while billionaire developers and industry-aligned political candidates are being routed by grassroots opposition. But beyond those running for or occupying political office, the backlash is also taking a toll on news networks viewed as pushing pro-data center propaganda. Case-in-point is Fox News , which has tailed president Donald Trump in embracing the AI industry’s narrative on data centers — an editorial decision which happens to coincides with viewers fleeing the network in droves. According to a new analysis by Media Matters for America, coverage spinning data centers in a positive light shot up by a staggering 420 percent across Fox News over the past two months. On August 18, a memo issued by the National Republican Senatorial Committee went out to party insiders and top corporate executives, warning that opposition to data centers presented a major challenge to the party’s victory in the upcoming US midterm elections. As Media Matters notes, Fox News quickly fell in line, increasing the total number of pro-data center claims to 203 between August 19 and September 2, compared to just 39 from August 5 through August 18. Bizarre claims of “far-left activists” and Chinese government propaganda likewise proliferated, teeing up Republican faithfuls to blame a boogeyman for the rise in anti-data center rhetoric. Surprisingly, the tactic appears to have backfired, as even the network’s most devoted acolytes reacted with disgust. “Just in case there were any dummies who thought Fox News cares what voters want,” one disaffected viewer wrote in the YouTube comments under an extremely sunny Fox and Friends segment on data centers. “They’ll always protect corporate interests over conservative interests and (perhaps) even over protecting Trump in certain cases.” “For the first time I’m going to say, FOX is GREEDY,” another angry viewer commented. “For people who like to say they believe in God, [they] sure are failing on following his word.” Recent reporting by Status found that viewership of Fox News is in freefall following the shift — plummeting down 27 percent across the month of October to an average of 1.1 million total viewers. That data comes from media tracking company Nielsen, which also noted that viewership across the months of July, August, and September shriveled by 16 percent compared to the previous three months. Viewers in the 24 to 54 age range — a crucial demographic — tumbled 24 percent over the period. While there are likely a litany of other reasons for the shift, it’s nonetheless a striking correlation that coincides with a broader falling out with Trump as president. American voters overwhelmingly disprove of his handling of the economy, not to mention the extremely costly war on Iran. With a crucial midterm election coming up, it remains to be seen how the backlash against the right’s embrace of third rail issues like data centers will cost Republicans at the polls. title: Anthropic says helping others is core to its mission. 3 philanthropy gurus say they'll believe it when they see it.
summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Chris Ratcliffe/Bloomberg/Getty Images Anthropic outlined several ways it plans to give back in its IPO filing this week. They include reserved shares, cofounder pledges, donation matching, and stock incentives. Philanthropy gurus said it's partly "reputation management," and how the money is used will be key. Anthropic's IPO filing this week contained myriad revelations about the state of the AI firm's finances, as well as an eye-opening series of claims about its commitment to helping others. We asked three experts in the world of philanthropy what they thought of these giving pledges. Their verdict: we'll see. A culture of giving? The company behind the AI chatbot Claude, which filed this week to go public in what could be the biggest IPO in history, laid out how it plans to give back and encourage its employees to do the same. Anthropic's seven cofounders said they've pledged 80% of their personal stock in the startup to charitable causes, gifts that could together be worth $80 billion. They also said they've earmarked 5% of Anthropic's equity for a "fund devoted to the public good," and plan to set aside another 2% for every sustained 50% rise in the company's stock price, with its IPO price as the base. Moreover, they said that new employees are offered a donation match, meaning that for every share they pledge to give away to good causes, Anthropic creates an additional share and matches the donation. Anthropic said that just over half of its employees have pledged at least some of their equity, including 70% of employees hired before May 2024, and nearly 50% of those hired after that date. title: Canceled port calls and cash appeals: Inside the final months of the Villa Vie Odyssey's doomed round-the-world cruise
summary: The Villa Vie Odyssey was bogged down by financial trouble in its final months at sea. Suy SE/AFP/Getty Images Villa Vie Residences promised residents the world. The company's cruise ship, the Odyssey, kept circling one corner of it while finances worsened, services deteriorated, and cash calls mounted. "We were going in a smaller and smaller circle," said Claude Sadovsky, who joined the Odyssey when it first set sail from Belfast in September 2024. "I signed up for a world cruise, and I was in purgatory." By early October, Sadovsky was frustrated enough with the itinerary changes that he left the ship and returned to his home in Maui. For Starr Davis, who also joined in Belfast in 2024, it was the constant appeals for fuel money that got her to jump ship in late September. "I got so sick of all the cash calls," she said. For those aboard the Odyssey in its final months, the crisis grew so acute that some passengers began fundraising for crew members, residents told Business Insider. The financial distress culminated in the ship's abrupt halt in Cambodia on Tuesday, when passengers were given eight hours to pack up their belongings and leave. While the speed of the end came as a shock to some, residents said signs of trouble had been growing. "The ship was just a pressure cooker," Davis said. "You know, 'Are we going to exist?'" In an interview with Business Insider on Friday, Villa Vie Residences cofounder and executive chairman Mikael Petterson confirmed the company had made cost-cutting changes. "There were itinerary changes," he said. "Of course there were." He said the changes aboard the Odyssey — home to a "never-ending" cruise for permanent residents who bought cabins for $119,999 to $439,999 — were driven by rising fuel costs and logistical challenges. "When you're the first one doing something, of course you're going to make a ton of mistakes," he said. Petterson said roughly 88% of Villa Vie is owned by residents; the rest is owned by the founders, management team, and him. A drawback of that structure is that residents were the ones turned to when money got tight, he said: "When there's money needed, residents are naturally called upon because there's no private equity. There's no big owner." "When things didn't go as planned, it was a double whammy," he added. "That is what made Villa Vie Residences so strong, yet so weak." Villa Vie Residences CEO Kathy Villalba did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Business Insider. In a now-deleted apology to residents, Villalba said Villa Vie was still speaking to potential investors and "holding onto whatever hope remains." Columbia Cruise Services, Villa Vie's operational partner, did not reply to several requests for comment. The round-the-world route started shrinking Villa Vie had marketed the three-and-a-half-year voyage as a circumnavigation with more than 425 port calls across 147 countries. For the period between October 2024 and October 2026, its initial itinerary listed 275 ports in 69 countries and territories, or 54 sovereign nations. As fuel costs rose after the onset of the war with Iran and Villa Vie's financial pressures worsened, the company increasingly pared down its route: It canceled stops, slowed the ship at sea, extended stays in ports, and revisited destinations to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs. To see how plans changed, Business Insider compared itineraries the ship issued at four different times: its initial itinerary from October 2024; its November 2025 itinerary, which showed where it went in 2024 and 2025; one from January 2026 showing changes before the war; and an October 2026 itinerary showing this year's stops. We also reviewed messages Villalba and Petterson sent to ship residents at various points over the past three months. Villa Vie Odyssey passengers in Cambodia after the voyage abruptly ended. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images We found that while the ship visited 54 nations between October 2024 and October 2026, it missed some territories and called at only 198 ports — 28% fewer than originally planned. Across the two years, our comparison of the itineraries showed the ship spent nearly two fewer months at sea than initially scheduled. Petterson blamed the skyrocketing price of fuel : "We had no choice," he said. Business Insider's analysis shows the Odyssey also made itinerary changes before fuel prices rose , including in Australia and New Zealand. Residents said those appeared to be for reasons other than fuel costs. Planning around an ever-changing itinerary For some residents, the route changes turned an around-the-world voyage into one long bout of déjà vu. "We have revisited some of the same ports countless times in the last several months," Angela Nuran Gokturk, 65, said. Messages from Petterson and Villalba to residents demonstrated how fuel, financing, and operating costs directly shaped the ship's route. In a message to residents on the ship's internal messaging platform on August 1, Villalba said they would cancel a stop in Brunei and sail directly from Singapore to Nha Trang in southern Vietnam "to conserve fuel and reduce operating costs." On August 7, Petterson said in a memo that the ship had "aggressively reduced costs" and "redesigned itineraries to spend more time in port and consume less fuel." In a message on September 6, Villalba said the Odyssey would extend its stay in Ha Long, Vietnam, by one or two days, depending on "fuel availability and funding." What was meant to be a three-night stay became a 10-night layover, the revised itinerary shows. Residents said the route changes made it difficult to plan flights and excursions in advance. "People stopped trying to make plans because things could change literally within a few days," said Sally Stunkel, 75, who joined the ship in February. During the stay in Ha Long , Stunkel joined an eight-person excursion to China, but the group had already booked flights to one of the Vietnamese stops that was later cut from the itinerary. They had to buy new tickets to rejoin the ship at its revised next port. "We spent more money trying to chase the ship, basically, to the next port so we could then board again," she said. The Villa Vie Odyssey had frequent itinerary changes. Suy Se / AFP via Getty Images Singapore became a repeat stop: The ship stopped there three times between May and July, spending 16 days there in total, according to the October 20 itinerary. Stunkel said the one change that frustrated her most was the removal of Japan and South Korea from the itinerary. In March, the ship's public itinerary showed it was supposed to visit 19 ports in Japan and South Korea, between June 26 and August 19. In April, the itinerary was updated to instead show stops in Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, and Brunei during that period. Stunkel said she had bought a cabin on the cruise in part because it was scheduled to visit Japan over the summer. She said she was "extremely disappointed" by the change, adding, "Japan is my No. 1 bucket list destination." Onboard services like dining and internet were hit Some onboard services were also disrupted. In a memo to residents on September 10, Villalba said that because the ship had fewer residents on board and fewer staff available, dining service would be consolidated. An on-board restaurant, The Palms, would temporarily close, while breakfast and lunch would be served buffet-style. Dinner would be a combination of à la carte and buffet. Davis said residents would joke when they went to dinner that it was "slim pickings." Starr Davis said the final months on the ship were like a "pressure cooker." Starr Davis Internet and TV services also suffered. Two residents said the internet had become spotty and unreliable. In a September 7 memo, Villalba said she had paid an outstanding balance and that internet service was being restored. Paul Montoya, 68, said the internet issues especially affected digital nomads living and working on the ship. Some would have to get off at port to find a nearby hotel with internet access, he said. Davis said air conditioning on the ship was throttled up or down pending fuel needs, adding, "Everything was about saving fuel." Petterson, who did not live on the ship and said he was not closely involved in its daily operations, said the company took measures to save money that went beyond conserving fuel. "We were cutting back where the residents would feel it the least, and that balance sometimes was difficult," he said. Residents were repeatedly asked to help keep the ship moving Management made repeated requests for residents to help cover Villa Vie's costs. In April, Villa Vie offered residents an "Emergency Loan Investment Opportunity," asking them to lend tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars to the company at interest rates of 12% to 24%, according to a letter viewed by Business Insider. Petterson said the request netted around $2 million that helped the ship survive for a few months. Aerial view of the Odyssey's pool deck. Villa Vie Odyssey From April onwards, Gokturk said it was "cash call after cash call." Gokturk and her husband did not participate in the loan program, she said, but they contributed to later appeals, including a voluntary fuel surcharge. "It became exhausting because it was constantly, 'Hey, we need more money. We need more money. If we don't get the money, then we're not going to be able to sail,'" Gokturk said. The uncertainty affected the mood aboard the ship . "It became very, very difficult," she said. Stunkel said the cash calls felt "incessant." She continued, "We felt like they were just leaching us out of whatever we had to keep the ship moving until the last possible moment." Four residents said that when they heard that staff had gone unpaid, they organized a fundraiser for the crew. Montoya said residents collected about $12,000 in cash outside the ship's café and distributed it to workers in $100 bills. There were several times in the last couple of months when payment owed to the crew was delayed, Petterson said, including by three weeks this month. He said as of around Wednesday, the crew had been paid. An employee in the Florida office said staff had received a partial payment, and that commissions hadn't been paid in months. Petterson said the company had been doing everything it could to keep the ship afloat. The company had tried to make the fuel surcharge mandatory but realized the residents' contracts didn't allow for it, so it became voluntary. Some residents contributed to the surcharge, while others bought additional discounted cabins through the VIP program. He said he had spent July looking for outside investment. By August, the situation was dire. A potential deal with Oneil Khosa, the former CEO of Margaritaville's cruise line, fell through last week. They were out of time. Business Insider was unable to reach Khosa for comment. In the days since the Odyssey's journey came to a halt in Cambodia, passengers have expressed a range of emotions. Some are heartbroken that their dream retirement came crashing to an end; others are hopeful the ship will sail again. One passenger said a group of fellow passengers is working on a "Hail Mary" attempt at buying the ship. Petterson said the focus is on a recapitalization, adding, "Preferably we need an operational partner that can come in with a stronger hand and a bigger pocket." Several residents said that despite how it ended, they don't regret the experience. But Sadovsky, who left before the Odyssey came to a halt, said the voyage he thought he had bought had become unrecognizable by the time he disembarked. "There was no reason for me to stay because I wasn't being exposed to new places anymore," he said. "I was revisiting the same old places, and I'd rather be home." Additional reporting by Amanda Goh. title: I'm running the NYC marathon along with four of my BI colleagues. These are our best tips for runners and spectators alike.
summary: BI's 2026 NYC marathon runners (left to right): Noah Sheidlower, Anthony DeMaio, Zak Jason, Kathleen Elkins, and Steve Russolillo BI This post originally appeared in the BI Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . Welcome to Marathon Sunday! Yours truly will be among nearly 60,000 runners taking on the five boroughs today. I've spent months training for this one — with a little help from Muse, Meta's AI agent. Several weeks ago, I wrote about how I had become addicted to Muse . Since then, Muse has become part of my marathon training, helping me map out long runs and shape an overall race plan. After the Staten Island half marathon last month, it even asked me, unprompted, "how'd the half go?" The other day, I gave Muse my bib number and asked it to track my run. I'm hoping for real-time feedback and analysis, delivered straight through my AirPods, on how my race is unfolding and how I can stay on pace to achieve my goals. But no AI agent can replicate the wisdom from real people. At Business Insider, five of us are running the NYC marathon this year. We range from a first-time marathoner (Discourse editor Zak Jason) to a true veteran in Anthony DeMaio on the sales team, who will be running his 23rd NYC marathon (and roughly his 40th overall marathon; he says he's lost count!) I asked them to share their best marathon advice for runners, spectators, or if you're simply trying to understand why someone would pay $330 to run 26.2 miles . Here's what they had to say: Noah Sheidlower , senior economy reporter: Live in the moment and acknowledge the spectators who came out to support. My race time last year was disappointing, but I had an absolute blast because I was high-fiving everyone and making people's days. Tap the "power up" marathon sign that little kids are holding, give a fist pump to strangers, and laugh when you see a funny sign that someone put a lot of effort into. The marathon shouldn't just be a celebration of your individual work but a community celebration honoring the greatest city on earth. Oh also, buy merch and don't feel guilty about it ! I bit the bullet and got the blue jacket, and it looks so good. Kathleen Elkins , investing correspondent : Soak it all in! title: I run an 8-person startup that uses AI agents. We don't let our agents run on vibes — here's the playbook system we created
summary: Rachel Woods created playbooks full of AI agents to replace additional hires at her company. Courtesy of Rachel Woods Rachel Woods taught herself AI while studying business in college, later landing a role at Facebook. She left to start her own business, which helps people integrate AI into their everyday workflows. She said the company has saved itself at least 4 new hires by using AI agents and playbooks. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rachel Woods, CEO and cofounder of AMP. The following has been edited for length and clarity. My first official role in AI was at Facebook. I started as an intern and then joined full-time in 2018. I worked on AI research and development for the ads system that's powered by AI. I don't have an engineering degree or background; I studied management information systems at The University of Texas at Austin. Part of why I think I got my role at Facebook was because I spent time building my own side projects and teaching myself how to train AI models and do data analysis. I left Facebook in 2020 to start my own business in the wine industry, and after that company sold, I founded an AI company. I would need to double the number of people on my team if we didn't use AI playbooks. If you're being thoughtful about setting up your AI operations, it's no different than building a team that you can trust. That's something a lot of people are missing: how to actually make these systems things you can take your eyes off and not keep yourself up at night in the process. Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents and bots, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form . I've been an entrepreneur since the age of 15 My first business was a photography business, and I was too young to even drive to meet my clients. I would always catch rides with people, and my parents hated this. I got into tech because in college, I was exposed to colleagues doing data analytics and working with coding and AI at summer internships. That led me to look online and try to take related classes, and I started to see that if you break a business problem into small enough pieces, you can get AI to handle parts of it: predicting, sorting, generating. Later, when I was applying to Facebook , I used AI and data analysis to build a report of coffee shops in Austin that were less likely to be too busy for me to study at. I think that project helped me land my role. After I left Facebook , I started a wine business called Vinebase in 2020; we built a tech platform that used AI to help winemakers sell their wine online and manage the digital side of their business. Because this was before AI became more mainstream, we didn't market it as AI. We called it our "auto magic" system. I think that if we had said it was AI, it could've been a turnoff for our customers. Vinebase was acquired by Corksy in fall 2022. I use my playbooks and AI agents to replace additional staff My sister and I started AMP, originally called The AI Exchange, before ChatGPT was released in November 2022, because I was using AI in Vinebase and saw how the technology was progressing. ChatGPT came out about a month later and started really accelerating the AI timeline, so we went all in. We have four full-time employees and four part-time contractors right now, but we'd need double if we weren't running as much as we are on AI. Given the company's current size, we'd need at least four to five additional people, including a sales and marketing manager, customer support specialist, executive assistant , and operations coordinator. The way we structure these systems is based on something we call playbooking. Every department in the company has its own system. Each system is a collection of playbooks with AI agents that can run independently or together. How we build our AI playbooks To build an AI playbook, pick one piece of work you do over and over, and write down what starts it, what goes into the task, and what should come out at the end. Next, write the steps the way you'd train a new hire: each step, the decisions in it, and what "good" looks like. Start running it with AI, and while you watch, compare the result to how you would've done it. Then, fix the playbook, not the output, until you trust it to run without you. I always think through how I want a playbook to work and outline it by hand. Whenever you're making an AI playbook, you want to own the thinking and the logic. Otherwise, you can fall into the trap of including something that you don't really understand, and then you're not going to be able to trust that system anyway. We have an AI agent running our sales playbook to review customer calls and ensure they meet our standards, rather than having a sales manager review them manually. Also, instead of sales team members needing to ask their manager questions, they just ask the playbook, which then pulls the answers from our guide for that team. There are two types of AI costs we have in the business. The first is the subscriptions to Claude and ChatGPT for every person on the team. The other is because the majority of our operations are these AI playbooks that are running in the background without us being the ones starting or triggering it. In September, we spent $8,510 on Claude Code to run our playbooks in the background, which is billed by usage and is separate from the team's monthly Claude and ChatGPT subscription costs. Own the playbook, rent the tech We say "own the playbook, rent the tech," which means that if you are creating really good playbooks for your AI to follow, it actually doesn't matter which tool you're running it in. Right now, we have a setup that's running with Claude Code in the background. But I could run all of these playbooks in ChatGPT, Grok, Gemini, or Microsoft Copilot . We try to avoid a lot of the risks that people are concerned about with AI going rogue by creating these detailed outlines. We don't just want the agents to run on vibes. There still needs to be a person to decide and design how the work gets done; AI just speeds up everything else. That's the job security we have in this AI era. Start small, and get everyone involved A few of us on the team who are more advanced with AI own the bigger, team-wide playbooks that the business depends on, but everyone playbooks their own personal workflow, and then we use that as the testing ground to graduate things into becoming more part of official systems. My advice would be to just start with something small and really easy, because once you get your first win and see how AI can do that repetitive work for you, it's kind of like a snowball. title: Apollo is sharing its private-equity  playbook with nonprofits
summary: The Apollo Global Management LLC office. Bloomberg/Getty Images Apollo Global Management gives portfolio companies operational guidance and leadership training. It also provides funding and operational support to 28 nonprofits, including a biennial training summit. The summit included discussions about the labor market and advice on making high-stakes decisions. Keeping up with AI and an uneven labor market is challenging enough for corporate leaders. For nonprofit executives working with tighter budgets and leaner teams, it can be extra daunting. "It's tricky for everyone right now, but for those guys, it's actually very tricky," Scott Kleinman, co-president of Apollo Asset Management and chair of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation Board. The foundation is addressing the challenges nonprofits face by providing 28 organizations with a version of the playbook Apollo uses with its over 190 portfolio companies, which include Yahoo Inc. and Shutterfly. That includes access to experts, leadership training , and a built-in network. The foundation also provides funding based on factors such as the organization's budget size and impact metrics. Apollo has so far provided over $13 million to grantees and committed to $100 million in funding over the next decade. The foundation, which launched in 2022, offered Business Insider an exclusive look at its biennial summit in October, where grantee leaders mingled with Apollo executives and sat in on panels led by subject-matter experts. Applying its portfolio playbook Kleinman said the foundation provides the same type of support it provides its portfolio companies, including operational guidance, data and digital transformation, talent management, and recruitment. "That is the crux of our foundation. Of course, it involves capital." Kleinman said, adding that the "real-value add" is the deal team. Each nonprofit is paired with a deal team of five to 10 employees from Apollo or Athene , which merged with Apollo and provides retirement services. Employees build relationships with the grantees to perform pro-bono projects, source board opportunities, and provide strategic advice. The foundation also holds monthly virtual training sessions to discuss topics like AI, leadership transitions, culture, real estate, fundraising, and succession planning. Beyond the funding At the October leadership summit, Apollo's chief economist Torsten Sløk discussed the labor market and how organizations can adapt to it, while the firm's chief financial officer talked about the factors nonprofits should consider when growing their organizations. The summit also included working sessions for grantees and their Apollo deal teams. The support Apollo offers grantees can be anything from fundraising skill-building to succession planning, said Lauren Coape-Arnold, Apollo Global Management's global head of citizenship and executive director of the Apollo Opportunity Foundation. She said the partnership starts with reorganizing boards to ensure strong governance, because an organization's success ultimately comes down to strong leadership. That may include sourcing candidates to consider for the board of directors or advisory board members. "Who is the leader? Do you believe in the leader? Are they someone inspiring the team to move forward?" Coape-Arnold said. What nonprofits need Jane Veron, cofounder and CEO of Acceleration Project, a nonprofit that helps small business owners said that support included identifying 35 processes the organization could eliminate or modify, from onboarding and technology to client data capture. For example, instead of having her team read through notes on a client's business challenges, Apollo is helping build an AI tool to do that work. It's also building asynchronous training tools to streamline consultant onboarding. "Apollo helped us identify priorities," Veron said, adding that the list includes "very micro and tactical" fixes. Reuben Ogbonna II, the cofounder and executive director of The Marcy Lab School, a one-year program that is an alternative to four-year college, said that meant revamping his school's curriculum to reflect the shifting roles of software engineers. He said Apollo's deal team helped them recognize that technologists need to work more closely with business leaders and integrated more business and industry context into the curriculum. The program also included additional cloud fundamentals and foundational DevOps knowledge, based on the team's input, he said. That sort of hands-on support is the goal, said Kleinman. "Not just to write some checks and get some photo ops, but to really make this a two-way street with our employees." Read the original article on Business Insider

title: Why pay $330 to run a marathon? Let me try to explain.
summary: The author during the 2021 NYC Marathon. Veranika Li This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. Between race registration fees and travel, I spend thousands of dollars a year on endurance events. It's money spent in alignment with my values, which experts say is the way to spend. You know the type of person who does run club? The one who wakes up before the sun on a Sunday to stack miles and finishes the run at a coffee shop, still sweating as they're waiting in line captioning their Strava post? That's me. I'm that person. I'm also among the group of people who spend a lot of money to safety-pin a number to their shirt and run from a start line to a finish line in exchange for a generic tech tee, a medal, and a banana. This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. I didn't bat an eye at checkout — not because I'm rich and the purchase wasn't significant. I'm not, and it was. But, to borrow one of Ramit Sethi's spending concepts , registration fees for endurance events would be one of my top " Money Dials ," which are essentially spending categories that you can either turn up or down. It's how I like to spend my discretionary income, and since I cut back in other areas, I can do so guilt-free, no matter how egregious the registration fee . I came up with the idea to write this particular story on a run. It was a Tuesday in June. I know the date because I left myself an eight-second voice memo recording the idea: "Why pay $300 for a marathon — to run 26.2 miles? Let me try to explain," I say, slightly out of breath. Why do I pay a lot of money to run marathons? And why the marathon — the 26.2-mile event? Why do I invest not only so much money but also so much time in training and racing? I'm not a professional, and never will be. My time is precious, but my chip time doesn't matter to anyone but me. For the past four months, I've pondered those questions — casually at first, and more urgently as the race (and the deadline for this article) approached. My first thought was to distinguish between running and racing. I picked up long-distance running in my early 20s, after more than a decade of junior tennis and four years of collegiate tennis had left me burned out on the sport. I was living in New York City, where finicky weather, high court fees, and complicated logistics make it difficult to hit a tennis ball, even if I wanted to. Looking for an affordable and efficient way to stay in shape, I turned to running. It was perfect for me: a minimalist who doesn't like stuff or clutter. I already had everything I needed: a pair of Nikes and easy access to a smooth running path. As an introvert, running suited me, giving me the time and space to think, plan, ideate, or simply check out of life's stressors. And the more I ran, the better I got at it. My marathon times started to suggest that I was decent at the distance — qualifying for the Boston Marathon is considered the pinnacle for amateur marathoners, a feat I've accomplished a few times — so maybe that's part of the reason I kept running, even if getting better made the activity a little more expensive. We all tend to gravitate toward the things we're good at, don't we? If running is meditative, rhythmic, and solitary, racing is exhilarating, hectic, and communal. It's a shared experience. You toe the line with thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of other runners. But unless you're vying for the podium, you're not competing against them. You're racing the clock and your past self — alongside, not against, thousands of others. Preparing for a marathon is challenging. It requires time, patience, and work — stacking miles and workouts for months. It's also incredibly satisfying. By the time race day rolls around, the hard part is done. When the gun goes off, the fun begins. NYRR If running is simple, efficient, and cheap, racing is coordinated, time-consuming, and expensive. That $333 entry fee was just the beginning of my expenses for this experience. I bought round-trip flights from Los Angeles and a really expensive pair of "super shoes" for race day. When I'm racing in a city where I don't have friends or family, hotels add up quickly. But back to Sethi and his "Money Dials," how you choose to spend your money matters. In fact, studies show that how you spend is oftentimes more important than how much you spend. Sethi's point is that, no matter your Money Dial — fitness, travel, experiences, or relationships — you can build a life that allows you to "spend extravagantly and unapologetically on the things that truly matter," while cutting costs "mercilessly" on the things that don't matter to you. Simply put: Spend on things that make you happy; don't spend on things that aren't important to you. The 2026 New York City Marathon will be my 21st marathon. summary_html:
The author during the 2021 NYC Marathon.

Veranika Li

  • This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon.
  • Between race registration fees and travel, I spend thousands of dollars a year on endurance events.
  • It's money spent in alignment with my values, which experts say is the way to spend.

You know the type of person who does run club? The one who wakes up before the sun on a Sunday to stack miles and finishes the run at a coffee shop, still sweating as they're waiting in line captioning their Strava post? That's me. I'm that person.

I'm also among the group of people who spend a lot of money to safety-pin a number to their shirt and run from a start line to a finish line in exchange for a generic tech tee, a medal, and a banana.

This summer, I spent $333.11 to register for the 2026 New York City Marathon. I didn't bat an eye at checkout — not because I'm rich and the purchase wasn't significant. I'm not, and it was. But, to borrow one of Ramit Sethi's spending concepts, registration fees for endurance events would be one of my top "Money Dials," which are essentially spending categories that you can either turn up or down. It's how I like to spend my discretionary income, and since I cut back in other areas, I can do so guilt-free, no matter how egregious the registration fee.

I came up with the idea to write this particular story on a run. It was a Tuesday in June. I know the date because I left myself an eight-second voice memo recording the idea: "Why pay $300 for a marathon — to run 26.2 miles? Let me try to explain," I say, slightly out of breath.

Why do I pay a lot of money to run marathons? And why the marathon — the 26.2-mile event? Why do I invest not only so much money but also so much time in training and racing? I'm not a professional, and never will be. My time is precious, but my chip time doesn't matter to anyone but me.

For the past four months, I've pondered those questions — casually at first, and more urgently as the race (and the deadline for this article) approached.

My first thought was to distinguish between running and racing.

I picked up long-distance running in my early 20s, after more than a decade of junior tennis and four years of collegiate tennis had left me burned out on the sport. I was living in New York City, where finicky weather, high court fees, and complicated logistics make it difficult to hit a tennis ball, even if I wanted to. Looking for an affordable and efficient way to stay in shape, I turned to running. It was perfect for me: a minimalist who doesn't like stuff or clutter. I already had everything I needed: a pair of Nikes and easy access to a smooth running path.

As an introvert, running suited me, giving me the time and space to think, plan, ideate, or simply check out of life's stressors. And the more I ran, the better I got at it. My marathon times started to suggest that I was decent at the distance — qualifying for the Boston Marathon is considered the pinnacle for amateur marathoners, a feat I've accomplished a few times — so maybe that's part of the reason I kept running, even if getting better made the activity a little more expensive. We all tend to gravitate toward the things we're good at, don't we?

If running is meditative, rhythmic, and solitary, racing is exhilarating, hectic, and communal. It's a shared experience. You toe the line with thousands — sometimes tens of thousands — of other runners. But unless you're vying for the podium, you're not competing against them. You're racing the clock and your past self — alongside, not against, thousands of others.

Preparing for a marathon is challenging. It requires time, patience, and work — stacking miles and workouts for months. It's also incredibly satisfying. By the time race day rolls around, the hard part is done.

When the gun goes off, the fun begins.

NYRR

If running is simple, efficient, and cheap, racing is coordinated, time-consuming, and expensive.

That $333 entry fee was just the beginning of my expenses for this experience. I bought round-trip flights from Los Angeles and a really expensive pair of "super shoes" for race day. When I'm racing in a city where I don't have friends or family, hotels add up quickly.

But back to Sethi and his "Money Dials," how you choose to spend your money matters. In fact, studies show that how you spend is oftentimes more important than how much you spend.

Sethi's point is that, no matter your Money Dial — fitness, travel, experiences, or relationships — you can build a life that allows you to "spend extravagantly and unapologetically on the things that truly matter," while cutting costs "mercilessly" on the things that don't matter to you.

Simply put: Spend on things that make you happy; don't spend on things that aren't important to you.

The 2026 New York City Marathon will be my 21st marathon. I keep track in the Notes app on my phone, recording my times, what I ate the night before, how many gels I consumed, and other random tidbits from the training block or race day.

What you get out of the race is entirely up to you. Your goal can be to run the fastest you ever have — a personal record, or "PR" — or it can be to simply cross the line with a smile on your face.

Of all the races I've done, the New York City Marathon is my favorite by far. Nearly 60,000 runners gather in Staten Island on the first Sunday of November to run through the city's five boroughs, absorbing high fives and hearty cheers from the millions of New Yorkers lining streets.

Anything can happen over the course of 26.2 miles, another component of the marathon's charm. You could cramp up and blow up. You could get an assist from a tailwind and negative split.

It's nearly impossible to have a perfect day, but sometimes race day magic strikes.

See you out there. Let's dial it up.

title: This new indie film about an AI startup founder and his family feels less like sci-fi by the day
summary: "Anna by the Window" is a film co-directed by filmmakers Myles Flusser and James Hyland. BaggySuit "Anna by the Window" is a coming-of-age film by filmmakers Myles Flusser and James Hyland. The film explores grief and human connection in the age of generative AI. Flusser said the film was at first a "speculative sci-fi" about AI, but then fiction became reality. From tech behemoths scrambling to replicate OpenAI's success with ChatGPT to Twitter rebranding to X under Elon Musk , Silicon Valley was undergoing an undeniable transformation in 2023. Nearly 3,000 miles away in New York, two skeptical 20-somethings were trying to make sense of it all. So, they made a film. "It was very personal," James Hyland, 25, told Business Insider. "We wanted to put something together that spoke to the things we were going through and what the world was like. That ended up being artificial intelligence and technological alienation." Hyland and Myles Flusser created "Anna by the Window," a coming-of-age film exploring grief and how technology can stifle human connection in the era of generative AI. The independent filmmakers wrote, directed, and produced the film in 2023 alongside their friends under their production company, Baggysuit. "Anna by the Window" is a coming-of-age film exploring grief and human connection in the digital era. Baggysuit "Particularly, it feels like the people running these platforms — YouTube, Instagram, et cetera — seem more contented than ever in letting it become a total slop apocalypse full of AI bots and non-human content," Flusser, 26, said. "That intrigues me in a way and scares me, obviously." Zoomers like Flusser and Hyland grew up inundated with smartphones, social media, and all the risks that come along with them. A year after they filmed "Anna by the Window," the US Surgeon General said social media should have a warning label because of its impact on mental health. Earlier this year, Meta settled a lawsuit brought by a coalition of states accusing it of designing platforms to addict children . The din of constant digital exposure has led some young folks to join the neo-Luddite movement , which takes a stand against overreliance on modern technology by emphasizing IRL human connection . Hyland is an organizer for a Luddite group called The Lamp Club . While the film was not made because of the Luddite movement, it shares many of its themes. "I think that it speaks to the synergy of our separate film project and this larger organizing project that's materializing all over the country, where people are fed up with these kinds of technological systems," Hyland said. When fiction becomes reality The "Anna by the Window" crew began screening the film in July. Baggysuit "Anna by the Window" is a glimpse inside the world of Ryan, a teenage boy who travels to New York City to reconnect with his older brother, James, the founder of an AI startup. The film's crew shot across New York State and used a variety of tools to bring the project to life, including ElevenLabs AI audio software to create the voice of Ryan and James' father throughout the film. The pair also pushed a real ChatGPT chatbot toward hallucination and included that audio in the film. "There's an AI chatbot that goes off the rails, you could say. We really cranked up all the dials," Hyland said. "It started saying 'error.' It started speaking different languages." Flusser said they wanted to portray the eerie nature of AI just right. They're not eager to use AI products in future projects, though. The majority of the film relies on traditional tools like a Sony camera, written outlines, and improv. "There's a strangeness and alienation that come up when we interact with chatbots and AI. We were trying to capture that feeling as purely as possible, so it felt totally necessary to use AI to do that," Flusser said. James Hyland and Myles Flusser used Eleven Labs and ChatGPT to create parts of the film. Baggysuit While aspects of the film are fictional, others pull directly from the directors' lives. "My brother had recently died. There's a lot of stuff in there that has to do with that," Flusser said. "There is a climactic moment between the two brothers in this movie that is actually surgically removed from my own life and recreated on screen." However, the way the filmmakers chose to characterize James in the film — delusional, stunted, running from reality — is distinct from Flusser's real brother. In the film, James is portrayed by Hyland, who said his version of an AI startup founder isn't based on a specific person. "My character was in a state of denial. Using this technology to be the thing that could deliver him closure or be the thing that he could connect with," Hyland said. "It makes him, in a way, kind of a sympathetic character." 'Anna by the Window' on the silver screen Hollywood is fixated on the real lives of tech founders . Production companies have backed films about SpaceX founder Elon Musk, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Meta founder Mark Zuckerberg, and former Theranos CEO Elizabeth Holmes . Even "Toy Story 5" tackled tech by introducing a smart tablet as the story's antagonist. "Anna by the Window" now joins the list of films putting the tech industry under a harsh microscope. "When we first started filming this, we were more mystified by AI, but toward the end our relationship with AI felt very cynical," Flusser said. "Anna by the Window" will become available to stream on Dolph on December 15. Baggysuit Watching AI evolve while creating a film about the technology was surreal, Hyland and Flusser said. "It was strange. When we were making it, we saw this movie as a speculative sci-fi about artificial intelligence," Flusser said. "Now, it's like nothing really is sci-fi about it anymore." The "Anna by the Window" crew began screening the film this summer in New York City and the Hudson Valley. There are upcoming screenings in Los Angeles this November. The film becomes available on Dolph, a streaming platform, beginning December 15. Read the original article on Business Insider
