title: Vibe coding is old news. People are 'vibe manufacturing' now.
summary: David Plakon prototyped an answering box for his kids with GPT-6 Astra. David Plakon These techies are using AI to prototype answering machines, toys, and jewelry. They call it "vibe manufacturing," a play on the term vibe coding. The vibe manufacturers are bullish on its potential. "AI literally does replace CAD engineering completely," one said. Jeff Deehan is a real estate developer by day and a "hobby guy" by night. The 42-year-old has a workshop in his East Lansing house. One project remained elusive: a small piece of steel to secure a camper to his truck. While Deehan was toying with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra in voice mode, he described the piece he needed and the angle at which it would sit. Five minutes later, the chatbot had prototyped it. GPT-6 Astra designed a steel part to secure a camper to Jeff Deehan's truck. Jeff Deehan Deehan told GPT-6 that he knew of a company called SendCutSend that does custom sheet-metal fabrication. The chatbot downloaded its design as a DXF file, opened SendCutSend's website, filled in the form, and paid the $156 with the payment information he'd stored. Ten days later, it was on his doorstep. "In about 10 minutes, I spoke a part out of my mind into existence, without touching my phone," he said. Deehan is part of a growing class of enthusiasts who are building physical gizmos with AI's help. They use chatbots to build prototypes, then send the AI-generated files to manufacturers, boutique fabricators, and their home 3D printers . Jeff Deehan ordered the truck piece from SendCutSend. It shipped in 10 days. Jeff Deehan Modeling physical items with AI has its risks. Deehan was sure his prototype would be a millimeter off here or there, though it ended up being right on. Other vibe manufacturers said that their products took multiple iterations, burning through their budgets. Normies have long used AI to write software, now dubbed " vibe coding ." These builders say AI is coming for hardware creation, too — and they're calling it "vibe manufacturing." A growing CADtastrophe Amy Zhou and Jake Fitzgerald are building an open-source tool for vibe manufacturing. They call it "text-to-CAD" — and it already tops 23,000 stars on GitHub. Zhou previously worked on the iPhone cases team at Apple and is now a design engineer at the AI rendering startup Vizcom. Fitzgerald wanted to get back into robotics after pivoting to crypto. They text new ideas back and forth between San Francisco and New York. The duo hopes to upend CAD, or computer-aided design . CAD engineers use software to design and optimize 3D models. It takes training and skill. The vibe manufacturers say you can do it easily with a large language model. Zhou makes jewelry with AI. The 25-year-old's previous startup turned pictures users uploaded into 3D models of charms, then cast the models in wax. It made a necklace for Cluely's CEO , Roy Lee, before Zhou left the business. She still occasionally makes AI-rendered charms for friends when they want necklaces of their pets. Amy Zhou turns photos into wax-cast jewelry with AI's help. Amy Zhou Fitzgerald is more interested in making robot arms. Using the text-to-CAD tool, the 31-year-old designed the arm in sheet metal and paid about $200 to have it built by SendCutSend. It has 0.6 meters of reach, with a motor and a camera, and he considers it an "edutainment" product to learn about robotics before the industry booms . A few months ago, Fitzgerald saw "compounding failures" when the AI would build bad designs on top of bad designs. The screw holes came in loose, for example. He spent about $2,000 repeatedly ordering pieces. With GPT-6 Astra, he said that's no longer a problem. Jake Fitzgerald prototyped a robot arm with his text-to-CAD AI tool. Jake Fitzgerald Sourish Sharma has watched AI change CAD. The 20-year-old from London got an MRI scan for a research study three years ago and asked for his data. He got a 3D printer and used an open-source tool to turn the data file into something printable. The tool didn't work very well, so he had to edit it by hand. "Some of the folds of the brain were not very foldy," he said. Now, Sharma has a much bigger printer — and AI. With one prompt, GPT-6 Astra blew the open-source tool out of the water, converting the data and making what he considers a more accurate brain. He's printed out a life-size one, as well as a handful of miniatures that he gives to friends. Sourish Sharma used AI to turn data from his MRI into a 3D-printed brain. Sourish Sharma "AI literally does replace CAD engineering completely," Sharma said. "It's kind of unfortunate if you're a CAD engineer. Fortunately, I'm not." The first audience: kids The more complex a product is, the more difficult it is to vibe manufacture. You won't be able to make a car at home with ChatGPT anytime soon. There's one population whose products are often simple and accessible: kids. Arthur Prince, a 34-year-old IT worker from outside Paris, said the children's toy he modeled in a week with AI would've taken him months with his CAD knowledge alone. Prince's toy creates stories and images with AI based on a kid's voice prompt. He developed everything, from the casing to the internal wiring, with GPT-6 Astra, then asked Claude to criticize its work. Once the two chatbots reached a consensus, he ordered 10 of the toys from the Chinese manufacturer JLCPCB for about 500 euros, fretting that he'd wasted his money on something that wouldn't work. Arthur Prince prototyped a toy for his daughter with GPT-6 Astra. Arthur Prince Luckily, they did. Prince's first tester, his daughter, loves it. "She's very proud to see that I can make something like this," he said. The benefit of vibe manufacturing kids' toys is their simplicity. Many parents don't want their children surfing the web , so AI prototypers don't have to worry about those pesky questions of cell service and web browsers. David Plakon wanted his kids to leave messages for their grandparents in Florida — but didn't want them on the internet. The 39-year-old from Austin is a longtime "tinkerer." He's had a 3D printer since 2015, and was printing his kid a " KPop Demon Hunters " sword while we spoke. So, he and his wife, Lara, figured they could build their own answering machine in the style of the Tin Can phone . David Plakon has printed the case for his answering box about 15 times. David Plakon Plakon gave GPT-6 Astra some design inspiration and instructions to build a prototype. All of the parts had to be purchasable or buildable with his 3D printer, he told the chatbot. It easily put together a model, instructing him to buy a potentiometer, a speaker, and an ESP32 chip, and guided him through the assembly. He's now printed the design some 15 times, improving it on each go. Initially, some of the pieces didn't fit together. "AI's good but not perfect," he said. David Plakon is still iterating on his voicebox, though the tech officially works. David Plakon But the box does work, and he hopes to sell it one day. He's keeping it small-scale for now, aiming to get the answering box in the grandparents' home for Christmas. "I don't have any delusion that I could send this to a factory, and they would be able to make it," Plakon said. "For now, it's very fun to prototype." Read the original article on Business Insider

David Plakon wanted his kids to leave messages for their grandparents in Florida — but didn't want them on the internet.

The 39-year-old from Austin is a longtime "tinkerer." He's had a 3D printer since 2015, and was printing his kid a "KPop Demon Hunters" sword while we spoke. So, he and his wife, Lara, figured they could build their own answering machine in the style of the Tin Can phone.

David Plakon has printed the case for his answering box about 15 times.

David Plakon

Plakon gave GPT-6 Astra some design inspiration and instructions to build a prototype. All of the parts had to be purchasable or buildable with his 3D printer, he told the chatbot. It easily put together a model, instructing him to buy a potentiometer, a speaker, and an ESP32 chip, and guided him through the assembly.

He's now printed the design some 15 times, improving it on each go. Initially, some of the pieces didn't fit together. "AI's good but not perfect," he said.

David Plakon is still iterating on his voicebox, though the tech officially works.

David Plakon

But the box does work, and he hopes to sell it one day. He's keeping it small-scale for now, aiming to get the answering box in the grandparents' home for Christmas.

"I don't have any delusion that I could send this to a factory, and they would be able to make it," Plakon said. "For now, it's very fun to prototype."

title: DoorDash's CEO: Don't be 'delusional' after just a few hundred AI agent orders
summary: Some third-party AI agents have generated "several hundred" DoorDash orders, CEO Tony Xu said. David Zalubowski/AP DoorDash isn't seeing many orders through AI agents like Muse yet, its CEO said. Third-party agents have generated "several hundred orders in total," Tony Xu said this week. Even so, DoorDash is moving ahead with its own AI ordering tools. The age of AI agents ordering your meals isn't here yet, according to DoorDash. The food delivery service has received "several hundred orders in total" from agents such as Meta's Muse, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said during the company's earnings call on Thursday. By comparison, DoorDash delivered 3.2 billion orders worldwide in 2025. Instead, customers are still using DoorDash's app and website to place orders, Xu said. "For the everyday ordering, what we see is people come to DoorDash, and they come back to DoorDash," he said. Xu's comments suggest that buzzy AI agents like Muse and Instinct have far to go before they become a big part of how users buy things. The agents can be useful for tracking the prices of holiday gifts or airline tickets, users told Business Insider earlier this month. Many are hesitant to let agents make the purchases themselves. They also use more secure payment options, such as single-use credit cards, in case the agents make a mistake. Despite the low order volume through third-party agents, DoorDash is making changes to its own AI tools. The company said in September that it was testing a text-to-order feature with an interface reminiscent of Instinct. Another ordering option, a chatbot called Ask DoorDash, creates an order from a recipe or shopping list and can adjust the contents to match customers' preferences. Those AI tools could eventually generate new orders on DoorDash, Xu said. "My take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity," he said. "But, at the same time, you do not want to be delusional," he added, referring to the low number of agent-placed orders. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? title: Nace AI Open-Sources Drex Max v1: A 27B Decision Model That Runs Locally on Apple Silicon
summary: Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights . Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF , an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama . For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine. TL;DR Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question. Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama. Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported). Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac. What is Drex Max? Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated . Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks. How does Drex Max work? The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence. Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window. &&& How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks? All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI, Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96. Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4. Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows. Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18. JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071). The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong. How do you run Drex Max locally? Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API. Runtime Hardware Checkpoint Images Python NVIDIA GPU bf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB) Yes llama.cpp fork Apple Metal, CPU Q8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB) No Ollama fork Apple Metal, CPU Q8_0 GGUF No Kapitsa v0.2.25+ Apple Silicon Q8_0 GGUF or affine Q4 No MLX Apple Silicon affine Q4 (14.45 GB) No The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa. Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile. Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips. summary_html:
Nace AI has released Drex Max v1 as open weights. Drex Max is its most capable decision model, and it now runs on your own hardware. The release ships bf16 weights, a Q8_0 GGUF, an affine Q4 checkpoint and forks of llama.cpp and Ollama. For developers, Drex Max open weights mean routing, classification and policy checks can stay on a local machine.

TL;DR
  • Size: Dense 27B parameters, 262,144-token window (16,384 by default), up to 255 options per question.
  • Runs on: NVIDIA GPU with Python (H100 bf16, or L40S 48 GB in 8-bit). Apple Silicon Macs with 24 GB+ (affine Q4) or 48 GB (Q8_0 GGUF). CPU via llama.cpp and Ollama.
  • Performance: 67.52 on the public Decision Index 0.4, 6.27 points ahead of Drex v2.0 (self-reported).
  • Best: 97.3 skill on InfographicVQA. Tools area reaches 81.9. A top-tier decision model you can now run offline on a Mac.
What is Drex Max?

Drex Max is a decision model from Nace.AI that answers typed questions about a given context. You pass a state (text, JSON or images) plus named questions. The model returns a probability for every option in one forward pass. Nothing is generated.

Questions come in 3 types: choice among named options, yes/no, and an ordinal score. That makes it a fit for agent routing, ticket triage and guardrail checks. The hosted version is presented at routing, classification and policy checks.

How does Drex Max work?

The model card describes a dense 27B backbone with 64 layers. 48 are Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers that run left to right. The other 16 are full-attention layers, placed every fourth layer, and they are non-causal. Every token can attend to the whole sequence.

Images pass through a native vision tower and are visible to every question in a request. A 255-way readout head then turns the last hidden state into option probabilities. The config lists a qwen3_5 model type with a 262,144-position window.

&&&

How does Drex Max perform on benchmarks?

All figures below are self-reported by Nace AI,

  • Decision Index 0.4 (public text): 67.52. Drex v2.0 scores 61.25 and Jev 1.13.0 scores 57.96.
  • Area skill: Tools 81.9, Language 72.2, Retrieval 68.8, Knowledge and Reasoning 57.1, Arts 53.4.
  • Public vision index: 73.92 across 11 benchmarks and 12,210 rows.
  • Artificial Analysis Decision Index: 64, which Nace says ranks 4th of 18.
  • JevBench: 92.2% (213/231). Decision Bench v4: 94.30% (1010/1071).

The results dataset covers 140,620 requests. Unanswered requests count as wrong.

How do you run Drex Max locally?

Nace documents 5 runtimes. All of them serve the same POST /v1/systemone API.

RuntimeHardwareCheckpointImagesPythonNVIDIA GPUbf16 (~49 GB) or 8-bit (~26 GB)Yesllama.cpp forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUF (27.25 GB)NoOllama forkApple Metal, CPUQ8_0 GGUFNoKapitsa v0.2.25+Apple SiliconQ8_0 GGUF or affine Q4NoMLXApple Siliconaffine Q4 (14.45 GB)No

The affine Q4 checkpoint targets Macs with 24 GB or more. The Q8_0 GGUF needs 48 GB. On a 48 GB Mac, Nace recommends –context 2048 for Kapitsa.

Ollama users set num_gpu 40 to offload 40 layers to Metal. Setting num_gpu 0 runs it on the CPU. The Ollama fork needs a CAPABILITY decision line in the Modelfile.

Quantization holds up in Nace’s tests. On a 48 GB Apple M5 Pro, the Q8_0 GGUF matched H100 bf16 within 0.02 per probability. The affine Q4 stayed within 0.0329 of Q8_0, with no choice flips.

Nace AI team states that Decision Index 0.4 uses the same public suite as 0.3.1. 

Key Takeaways
  • Drex Max v1 weights are now public under Nace.AI Open RAIL-M.
  • It scores 67.52 on Decision Index 0.4, above Drex v2.0 (61.25).
  • A 4-bit build runs on 24 GB Apple Silicon Macs via Kapitsa or MLX.
  • Q8_0 on an M5 Pro matched H100 bf16 within 0.02.
  • Local Mac and CPU paths are text only for now.

title: DeepSeek Open-Sources dsh-superagent, a Router-Worker Coding Agent
summary: The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent , an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness . It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System . TL;DaR What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to. Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+. Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent. Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster). Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured. What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent? It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person. The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure. Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent? DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng , a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking. How does the Router-Worker architecture work? The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work. In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model : Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events. Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work. Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed. Subscription: later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention. The main session runs the dsh-superagent-router preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs dsh-superagent-worker . Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the execution doc . Proactive work is gated. The authorization doc defines 3 accept modes: off , observe (default) and auto . In observe , the agent only records what it would have accepted. The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop. && How does it perform? DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per ifeng’s account of the report . Super-agent: p50 of 12.4 minutes, p95 of 15.7 minutes. Single session plus subagents, neutral prompt: p95 of 29.5 minutes. No p50 was given. Why: under the neutral prompt, the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs . Router load: as arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8. Per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds. An ablation removed direct event pass-through. Router decisions rose about 30%, and cache-read tokens rose about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M . All figures are self-reported and come from secondary reports of the report. How does dsh-superagent compare with other GitHub coding agents? A Router dispatches work; isolated Worker sessions execute each Ticket. Simulated p95 task time: 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for a single session. Proactive work stays in observe mode until a team switches it on. It runs with full OS-user access, so isolate it before use. Check out the GitHub repo , the setup guide and the design docs . summary_html:
The DeepSeek Harness team just released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed research prototype. DeepSeek dsh-superagent is a proactive coding agent for one GitHub repository. It is packaged as a bundle for DeepSeek Harness. It listens to GitHub and, optionally, Feishu. It turns allowed requests into parallel work items, each in its own agent session. The release shipped alongside a design post, Exploring Super-agent Design: Towards a More Autonomous Agent System.

TL;DaR
  • What is it?: A TypeScript bundle, v0.1.0, released as 1 commit under MIT. It uses whatever model the Harness profile is set to.
  • Runs on: Your own machine, as a dedicated DeepSeek Harness profile. Needs Node.js 22.19+ or 24+, git 2.32+, Python 3.8+, tmux and GitHub CLI 2.48+.
  • Performance: In DeepSeek’s simulation, it finished tasks far faster under a noisy message stream than a single-session agent.
  • Best: p95 task completion of 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for the single-session baseline (about 1.9x faster).
  • Worst: Tested only on synthetic messages and simulated tools. Real coding quality was not measured.
What is DeepSeek dsh-superagent?

It is a GitHub agent that waits to be asked. When an allowed person addresses it, it opens a work item, called a Ticket. Each Ticket runs in its own session and directory. Results return to the original conversation, often as a pull request. A local web panel lists only what needs a person.

The README page states the core rule plainly: take as little human attention as possible, and give as much value as possible. The philosophy doc applies it to behavior. The agent confirms once, stays quiet while working, and writes again only with a result, a question or a failure.

Why did DeepSeek build a Super-agent?

DeepSeek team argues that mainstream agents treat 1 session as the basic unit. According to the report, as reported by ifeng, a person can actively follow only 3 to 5 sessions at once. Human attention, not model capability, becomes the bottleneck for multitasking.

How does the Router-Worker architecture work?

The research team describes 2 layers. A long-running Router handles interaction and dispatch. Isolated Worker sessions do the actual work.

In the prototype, that flow is concrete, per the domain model:

  • Source → Trigger: GitHub or Feishu produces events.
  • Eval: decides whether a batch of Triggers asks for new work.
  • Ticket: a unit of authorized work, with an immutable Mandate stating why it may proceed.
  • Subscription: later comments on a pull request reach the right Worker without a fresh mention.

The main session runs the dsh-superagent-router preset with a smaller tool set. Each Worker runs dsh-superagent-worker. Shell commands move to the background after 5 seconds, so Workers keep receiving messages, per the execution doc.

Proactive work is gated. The authorization doc defines 3 accept modes: off, observe (default) and auto. In observe, the agent only records what it would have accepted.

The research team also lists ideas beyond the prototype: an external Watchdog, storage and compute separation, and an asynchronous ReAct loop.

&&

How does it perform?

DeepSeek tested with simulated group chat and GitHub CI streams. Each run had about 300 messages, of which about 20 were real work requests. Each scheme ran 5 times, per ifeng’s account of the report.

  • Super-agent: p50 of 12.4 minutes, p95 of 15.7 minutes.
  • Single session plus subagents, neutral prompt: p95 of 29.5 minutes. No p50 was given.
  • Why: under the neutral prompt, the baseline called a subagent 0 times in 5 runs.
  • Router load: as arrivals rose from about 1 to 40 per minute, batch size grew from 1.0 to 2.8. Per-request latency rose from 2.5 to 3.9 seconds.

An ablation removed direct event pass-through. Router decisions rose about 30%, and cache-read tokens rose about 37%, from 23.23M to 31.77M. All figures are self-reported and come from secondary reports of the report.

How does dsh-superagent compare with other GitHub coding agents?   • DeepSeek released dsh-superagent, an MIT-licensed proactive coding agent prototype.
  • A Router dispatches work; isolated Worker sessions execute each Ticket.
  • Simulated p95 task time: 15.7 minutes vs 29.5 minutes for a single session.
  • Proactive work stays in observe mode until a team switches it on.
  • It runs with full OS-user access, so isolate it before use.

title: # Anima Memory Vault: Keeping Family Stories Alive with a Local Spirit Guardian
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine What I Built Anima Memory Vault is a Día de los Muertos-inspired family memory application that preserves oral history through an interactive digital ofrenda. Users can: Add memories, recipes, traditions, and family stories. Store them in MongoDB Atlas. Ask questions about their family history. Retrieve relevant memories using vector search. Receive answers from a warm ancestor-spirit persona. Listen to responses through ElevenLabs narration or the browser's local speech synthesis. I interpreted “Ghost in the Machine” as a gentle presence of memory: not a frightening ghost, but a spirit guardian that helps keep family voices, traditions, and stories alive. Demo Code Check Github Code How I Built It The application uses: React with Vite for the frontend. Node.js and Express for the backend. MongoDB Atlas Vector Search for memory retrieval. Ollama for local AI inference. gemma2:2b for generating ancestor-spirit responses. nomic-embed-text for converting memories and questions into embeddings. ElevenLabs for optional voice narration. The browser Web Speech API as an offline narration fallback. The RAG flow works like this: Family memory ↓ nomic-embed-text creates an embedding ↓ Embedding is stored in MongoDB Atlas ↓ User asks a question ↓ The question is embedded ↓ MongoDB Vector Search retrieves related memories ↓ Retrieved memories are provided to gemma2:2b ↓ The spirit guardian generates a grounded answer The application also supports a local in-memory fallback when MongoDB is not configured, allowing the project to run completely locally during development. One important design decision was to instruct the model not to invent family history: If the retrieved memories do not contain the answer, the spirit guardian should say so gently instead of creating facts. This keeps the responses respectful and grounded in the memories that users actually provided. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation made it possible to build a private, meaningful memory experience using local models instead of sending family stories to a closed AI service by default. Using Ollama means the core generation and embedding workflow can run locally: Family memories can remain on the user's machine during development. The project can work without a paid AI API. Developers can experiment with different open-weight models. The retrieval and generation pipeline is transparent and customizable. The application can fall back gracefully when cloud services are unavailable. MongoDB Atlas adds persistent vector search, while the local Ollama models provide the intelligence behind the experience. ElevenLabs is an optional enhancement for more natural narration. If it is unavailable, the application falls back to the browser's native speech synthesis. The Spirit of It The most meaningful part of the project is that the “ghost” is not treated as something scary. The spirit guardian represents the way family memories continue to speak through recipes, songs, sayings, places, and small traditions. A question such as: What did Abuela Rosa prepare every November? can bring a stored memory back into the conversation and make the family story feel present again. Anima Memory Vault is designed to feel like lighting a candle: a small act of remembrance that keeps someone’s story from disappearing.
summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

Anima Memory Vault is a Día de los Muertos-inspired family memory application that preserves oral history through an interactive digital ofrenda.

Users can:

  • Add memories, recipes, traditions, and family stories.
  • Store them in MongoDB Atlas.
  • Ask questions about their family history.
  • Retrieve relevant memories using vector search.
  • Receive answers from a warm ancestor-spirit persona.
  • Listen to responses through ElevenLabs narration or the browser's local speech synthesis.

I interpreted “Ghost in the Machine” as a gentle presence of memory: not a frightening ghost, but a spirit guardian that helps keep family voices, traditions, and stories alive.

Demo

Code

Check Github Code

How I Built It

The application uses:

  • React with Vite for the frontend.
  • Node.js and Express for the backend.
  • MongoDB Atlas Vector Search for memory retrieval.
  • Ollama for local AI inference.
  • gemma2:2b for generating ancestor-spirit responses.
  • nomic-embed-text for converting memories and questions into embeddings.
  • ElevenLabs for optional voice narration.
  • The browser Web Speech API as an offline narration fallback.

The RAG flow works like this:

Family memory
    ↓
nomic-embed-text creates an embedding
    ↓
Embedding is stored in MongoDB Atlas
    ↓
User asks a question
    ↓
The question is embedded
    ↓
MongoDB Vector Search retrieves related memories
    ↓
Retrieved memories are provided to gemma2:2b
    ↓
The spirit guardian generates a grounded answer

The application also supports a local in-memory fallback when MongoDB is not configured, allowing the project to run completely locally during development.

One important design decision was to instruct the model not to invent family history:

If the retrieved memories do not contain the answer, the spirit guardian should say so gently instead of creating facts.

This keeps the responses respectful and grounded in the memories that users actually provided.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation made it possible to build a private, meaningful memory experience using local models instead of sending family stories to a closed AI service by default.

Using Ollama means the core generation and embedding workflow can run locally:

Family memories can remain on the user's machine during development.
The project can work without a paid AI API.
Developers can experiment with different open-weight models.
The retrieval and generation pipeline is transparent and customizable.
The application can fall back gracefully when cloud services are unavailable.
MongoDB Atlas adds persistent vector search, while the local Ollama models provide the intelligence behind the experience.

ElevenLabs is an optional enhancement for more natural narration. If it is unavailable, the application falls back to the browser's native speech synthesis.

The Spirit of It

The most meaningful part of the project is that the “ghost” is not treated as something scary.

The spirit guardian represents the way family memories continue to speak through recipes, songs, sayings, places, and small traditions. A question such as:
What did Abuela Rosa prepare every November?

can bring a stored memory back into the conversation and make the family story feel present again.

Anima Memory Vault is designed to feel like lighting a candle: a small act of remembrance that keeps someone’s story from disappearing.

title: On 21 Nov 2024 Adani fell 22.61%. My model didn't know why, and it wasn't allowed to guess.
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine In our house, the stock market is dinner-table conversation. And after every truly ugly red day, I hear the same sentence: "Nobody could have seen that coming." I always wanted to ask: how unexpected was it, really? Not "it fell a lot", but how far outside normal it was for that stock , given everything it had done before. So I built something that answers exactly that question. It doesn't read the news. All it knows is a stock's own past. Then I pointed it at 21 November 2024 . That day, Adani Enterprises fell 22.61% . Going in, my model had studied 750 days of the stock's history and drawn the line for a truly terrible day at about −10% . The real day went more than twice as far. The model couldn't say why. It could only say: this day should not have been possible. That's a ghost. I built a machine to hunt them. What I Built Ghost Candles looks back through any Indian stock's history, finds the days its own past could not explain, and gives each one a ghost story. It has two AI models with very different jobs: The Oracle ( TabPFN-3.5 , running on my laptop): for every trading day, it looks only at the days before it and predicts a range of likely moves, like a weather forecast for a stock: "98% sure tomorrow lands between −10% and +9%." The ghosts: if the real move lands far outside that range, with odds of 1 in 100 or worse, the day becomes a Poltergeist . If it breaks past the very edge of the forecast, it's a Wraith . The Medium (Google's Gemma, running locally through Ollama): writes a short ghost story for each one. It gets the numbers and one unbreakable rule: you do not know why this happened, so you may never give a reason. Everything ends up in one web page: a chart with glowing ghosts, a card and story for each, and an honesty check on the Oracle. Demo Click a glowing dot and read its ghost: Adani Enterprises: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/ADANIENT_NS.html Reliance Industries: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/RELIANCE_NS.html The night the Wraith walked TabPFN expected 21 November 2024 to land somewhere between −9.92% and +8.98% . It fell 22.61% , on 19.8 times the usual trading volume. I know what happened that day: the group's shares crashed after news that US prosecutors had charged its chairman. The model doesn't know that, and Gemma isn't allowed to guess. Ghost Candles doesn't explain the past. It points at the exact moment an explanation was needed. It happened with Reliance too, two nights in a row: Monday, 3 June 2024: +5.59% . TabPFN rated it 1 in 215. Tuesday, 4 June 2024: −7.49% . TabPFN rated it 1 in 327. Those are the exit-poll rally and the results-day crash of India's 2024 general election. The model has never heard of an election. It just knew both days were wrong. Here's a piece of what Gemma wrote for the Wraith: The candle, a fractured thing of obsidian, plummeted. The model, a pale imitation of prediction, shuddered with an impossibility. The record: -22.61% on 2024-11-21, with a model's odds of approximately 1 in 1,000+ that the move would occur. The story can be dramatic. "The record" line always states the plain facts. The First Reader: Our Dinner Table I showed the live Adani page to the person at our dinner table who trades every day, the one who usually says "nobody could have seen that coming." Here's what they told me (paraphrased): On 21 November 2024: Of course they remembered it. Next to TabPFN's −9.92% to +8.98% range, the real −22.61% made them agree: the model was right to call it impossible. The catch: a seasoned quant would shrug, because ranges built from history always break in a panic. On the quiet 23 July 2026 ghost: Not impressed. Sleepy low-volume dips happen all the time in Indian markets; flag too many and people close the tab. On using it every week: They wouldn't. If your stock falls 22%, you already watched it happen. Unless it warns you before , it's a clever post-mortem. All three are fair. The big ghosts are where it earns its keep: it measures how abnormal a day was, without hindsight, even though it can't say why . Quiet ghosts need a higher bar, so the next version should require a minimum move or a volume spike. And yes, it's a post-mortem; I'm not claiming otherwise. How I Built It 1. Turning candles into a table TabPFN is built for tables, so each trading day becomes one row of 17 columns describing the stock up to the night before : recent returns, how jumpy it had been, how busy trading was, how far it sat from its 50-day average, and so on. That "night before" rule matters most: if the model could see even a hint of the day it's predicting, nothing would look surprising, and there would be no ghosts. 2. Never letting it peek at the future The Oracle learns from the previous 750 trading days, forecasts the next 20, then slides forward: 34 rounds and 671 forecast days per stock, each one a forecast it could really have made at the time. TabPFN makes this cheap. It's pretrained on millions of made-up tables and learns a new table just by reading it, so there's no training and I didn't tune a single setting. With TabPFN-3.5-Fast it ran on my i3 laptop with no GPU : about 11 minutes for Adani, 18 for Reliance. 3. A range, not a single guess This one line is what the whole project stands on: quantiles = model . predict ( X_test , output_type = " quantiles " , quantiles = LEVELS ) Most models give one number: "tomorrow: +0.3%". You can't call a day impossible without knowing what was possible . TabPFN gives the whole spread, from the 0.1% worst case to the 99.9% best case. Where the real day landed in that spread becomes its odds. 4. Can the Oracle be trusted? A ghost detector is only as good as its sense of "normal". If its ranges are too narrow, everything looks haunted. So I compared TabPFN against the textbook shortcut almost everyone uses: assuming daily moves follow a bell curve. Adani Enterprises, 671 forecast days: TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 4 24 Its "98% sure" range actually held 99.0% 95.1% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 34.7 36.5 Reliance Industries, 671 forecast days: TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 5 16 Its "98% sure" range actually held 98.4% 96.4% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 20.3 20.4 In plain words: The bell curve panics. On Adani it shouted "1 in 100!" 24 times, more than three times what luck alone would produce. Its "98% sure" range was really about 95% sure, so it's overconfident exactly where ghosts live. TabPFN stays calm, and is right to. It flagged 4 and 5 ghosts, close to what an honest forecaster should. It wins clearly on the wild stock and only barely on the calm one. On Adani its overall error is about 5% lower. On Reliance it's essentially a tie. It's slightly too careful. Its ranges ran a little wide (99% instead of 98%), so it may miss a ghost rather than invent one. That's the right mistake. It sees things the bell curve can't. On 23 July 2026, Adani dipped 4.37% on a quiet day. The bell curve said 1 in 27; TabPFN, knowing how calm the stock had been, said 1 in 102. (My first reader wasn't convinced that kind of ghost matters. Fair.) 5. The storyteller needed a fact-checker My first storyteller, the tiny gemma3:1b , never invented a reason, but it was terrible with numbers. It turned a +5.26% day into "nearly eight percent" and a −10.65% crash into "a single negative percentage point" . So before any story reaches the page, a small checker reads it and sends it back if it: uses any number that wasn't in the facts it was given, spells a number out in words (which can't be checked), names a possible cause like earnings, an election or news, runs too long, or forgets the plain "The record:" line at the end. Gemma gets three tries. If it still fails, the page shows a plain factual summary instead. Even with the bigger gemma3:4b , the checker rejected 12 of 17 drafts . Many were just too long, but some were sneaky: It invented share prices ("the open price was 188.73, the close 199.33") that appear nowhere in its facts. Told not to write numbers as words, it turned "8.6x normal volume" into "eight hundred and sixty unseen hands" . Gemma wrote 5 of the 9 stories; the other 4 are plain summaries. A boring true sentence beats a spooky false one. 6. The page The journal is one HTML file with no outside scripts, hosted free on GitHub Pages. I used an AI coding assistant to help write and debug the code; every run, number and story here comes from running it myself. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? It's free to run, again and again. Hundreds of model calls across my testing, with no API bill and no rate limits. Your watchlist stays yours. The stocks you look up say a lot about you. Here nothing leaves the laptop. I can open up every part. TabPFN gives me its full range of outcomes. When the small Gemma got numbers wrong, I swapped in a bigger one with one flag and wrapped it in my own checker, and I can read every rejected draft. It can't be switched off. Both models are files on my disk, which felt right for a project about things that refuse to stay dead. Who Could Use This, and How It Would Scale Under the ghost stories is a useful idea: a surprise score for every stock, measured against its own normal . A 3% drop in a sleepy stock can mean more than 6% in a wild one, and a "top losers" list can't tell the difference. Investors could check which holdings did something truly abnormal; analysts could find the strange days first, then read the news for just those; surveillance teams look for exactly the shape of 21 November 2024, a huge unexpected move on heavy volume. My first reader is right that nobody opens a post-mortem weekly. The version worth building is a nightly scan: one forecast per stock ("was today a ghost?") across a watchlist or a whole exchange, with Gemma writing only for the few ghosts. What stands in the way: TabPFN-3.5's weights are non-commercial, so a paid product would need a commercial licence, and two stocks is far too little evidence. What It Isn't Not a trading signal and not financial advice. It tells you a day was strange, not that tomorrow will be. Moves past the forecast's edge show as "1 in 1,000+", not a precise number the model can't back up. Code BhaktiKa / ghost-candles Ghost Candles Find the days a stock did something its own past said was nearly impossible, and let a local model tell their ghost stories. Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine . The Oracle: TabPFN-3.5 , an open-weight tabular foundation model, runs locally. For every trading day it forecasts a full probability distribution of that day's return, using only data from before that day (walk-forward, refit every 20 days on the previous 750). The Ghosts: any day whose actual move had odds of 1 in 100 or worse under the Oracle's forecast. Beyond the 0.1% / 99.9% quantiles it becomes a Wraith . The Medium: a local open-weight LLM (default Google Gemma gemma3:4b via Ollama ) writes a short ghost story for each one. It only gets the numbers and is told it does not know why the move happened, so it… View on GitHub Try it on any NSE or BSE stock: python haunt.py TATAMOTORS.NS --version v3.5-fast python renarrate.py out/TATAMOTORS_NS.json --llm gemma3:4b Prize Categories Best Use of TabPFN: TabPFN-3.5 is the Oracle. It runs locally in a no-peeking forecasting loop, its full range of outcomes decides what counts as a ghost, and it's tested honestly against a bell-curve baseline on two stocks. Best Use of Gemma: Gemma runs locally via Ollama as the storyteller, inside a fact-check-and-retry loop that keeps its stories truthful.
summary_html:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

In our house, the stock market is dinner-table conversation. And after every truly ugly red day, I hear the same sentence:

"Nobody could have seen that coming."

I always wanted to ask: how unexpected was it, really? Not "it fell a lot", but how far outside normal it was for that stock, given everything it had done before.

So I built something that answers exactly that question. It doesn't read the news. All it knows is a stock's own past.

Then I pointed it at 21 November 2024.

That day, Adani Enterprises fell 22.61%. Going in, my model had studied 750 days of the stock's history and drawn the line for a truly terrible day at about −10%. The real day went more than twice as far. The model couldn't say why. It could only say: this day should not have been possible.

That's a ghost. I built a machine to hunt them.

What I Built

Ghost Candles looks back through any Indian stock's history, finds the days its own past could not explain, and gives each one a ghost story.

It has two AI models with very different jobs:

  • The Oracle (TabPFN-3.5, running on my laptop): for every trading day, it looks only at the days before it and predicts a range of likely moves, like a weather forecast for a stock: "98% sure tomorrow lands between −10% and +9%."
  • The ghosts: if the real move lands far outside that range, with odds of 1 in 100 or worse, the day becomes a Poltergeist. If it breaks past the very edge of the forecast, it's a Wraith.
  • The Medium (Google's Gemma, running locally through Ollama): writes a short ghost story for each one. It gets the numbers and one unbreakable rule: you do not know why this happened, so you may never give a reason.

Everything ends up in one web page: a chart with glowing ghosts, a card and story for each, and an honesty check on the Oracle.

Demo

Click a glowing dot and read its ghost:

  • Adani Enterprises: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/ADANIENT_NS.html
  • Reliance Industries: https://bhaktika.github.io/ghost-candles/out/RELIANCE_NS.html

The night the Wraith walked

TabPFN expected 21 November 2024 to land somewhere between −9.92% and +8.98%. It fell 22.61%, on 19.8 times the usual trading volume.

I know what happened that day: the group's shares crashed after news that US prosecutors had charged its chairman. The model doesn't know that, and Gemma isn't allowed to guess. Ghost Candles doesn't explain the past. It points at the exact moment an explanation was needed.

It happened with Reliance too, two nights in a row:

  • Monday, 3 June 2024: +5.59%. TabPFN rated it 1 in 215.
  • Tuesday, 4 June 2024: −7.49%. TabPFN rated it 1 in 327.

Those are the exit-poll rally and the results-day crash of India's 2024 general election. The model has never heard of an election. It just knew both days were wrong.

Here's a piece of what Gemma wrote for the Wraith:

The candle, a fractured thing of obsidian, plummeted. The model, a pale imitation of prediction, shuddered with an impossibility.

The record: -22.61% on 2024-11-21, with a model's odds of approximately 1 in 1,000+ that the move would occur.

The story can be dramatic. "The record" line always states the plain facts.

The First Reader: Our Dinner Table

I showed the live Adani page to the person at our dinner table who trades every day, the one who usually says "nobody could have seen that coming." Here's what they told me (paraphrased):

  • On 21 November 2024: Of course they remembered it. Next to TabPFN's −9.92% to +8.98% range, the real −22.61% made them agree: the model was right to call it impossible. The catch: a seasoned quant would shrug, because ranges built from history always break in a panic.
  • On the quiet 23 July 2026 ghost: Not impressed. Sleepy low-volume dips happen all the time in Indian markets; flag too many and people close the tab.
  • On using it every week: They wouldn't. If your stock falls 22%, you already watched it happen. Unless it warns you before, it's a clever post-mortem.

All three are fair. The big ghosts are where it earns its keep: it measures how abnormal a day was, without hindsight, even though it can't say why. Quiet ghosts need a higher bar, so the next version should require a minimum move or a volume spike. And yes, it's a post-mortem; I'm not claiming otherwise.

How I Built It 1. Turning candles into a table

TabPFN is built for tables, so each trading day becomes one row of 17 columns describing the stock up to the night before: recent returns, how jumpy it had been, how busy trading was, how far it sat from its 50-day average, and so on. That "night before" rule matters most: if the model could see even a hint of the day it's predicting, nothing would look surprising, and there would be no ghosts.

2. Never letting it peek at the future

The Oracle learns from the previous 750 trading days, forecasts the next 20, then slides forward: 34 rounds and 671 forecast days per stock, each one a forecast it could really have made at the time.

TabPFN makes this cheap. It's pretrained on millions of made-up tables and learns a new table just by reading it, so there's no training and I didn't tune a single setting. With TabPFN-3.5-Fast it ran on my i3 laptop with no GPU: about 11 minutes for Adani, 18 for Reliance.

3. A range, not a single guess

This one line is what the whole project stands on:

quantiles = model.predict(X_test, output_type="quantiles", quantiles=LEVELS)

Most models give one number: "tomorrow: +0.3%". You can't call a day impossible without knowing what was possible. TabPFN gives the whole spread, from the 0.1% worst case to the 99.9% best case. Where the real day landed in that spread becomes its odds.

4. Can the Oracle be trusted?

A ghost detector is only as good as its sense of "normal". If its ranges are too narrow, everything looks haunted. So I compared TabPFN against the textbook shortcut almost everyone uses: assuming daily moves follow a bell curve.

Adani Enterprises, 671 forecast days:

TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 4 24 Its "98% sure" range actually held 99.0% 95.1% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 34.7 36.5

Reliance Industries, 671 forecast days:

TabPFN Bell curve Ghosts flagged (pure luck would give about 7) 5 16 Its "98% sure" range actually held 98.4% 96.4% Overall forecast error (lower is better) 20.3 20.4

In plain words:

  • The bell curve panics. On Adani it shouted "1 in 100!" 24 times, more than three times what luck alone would produce. Its "98% sure" range was really about 95% sure, so it's overconfident exactly where ghosts live.
  • TabPFN stays calm, and is right to. It flagged 4 and 5 ghosts, close to what an honest forecaster should.
  • It wins clearly on the wild stock and only barely on the calm one. On Adani its overall error is about 5% lower. On Reliance it's essentially a tie.
  • It's slightly too careful. Its ranges ran a little wide (99% instead of 98%), so it may miss a ghost rather than invent one. That's the right mistake.
  • It sees things the bell curve can't. On 23 July 2026, Adani dipped 4.37% on a quiet day. The bell curve said 1 in 27; TabPFN, knowing how calm the stock had been, said 1 in 102. (My first reader wasn't convinced that kind of ghost matters. Fair.)
5. The storyteller needed a fact-checker

My first storyteller, the tiny gemma3:1b, never invented a reason, but it was terrible with numbers. It turned a +5.26% day into "nearly eight percent" and a −10.65% crash into "a single negative percentage point".

So before any story reaches the page, a small checker reads it and sends it back if it:

  • uses any number that wasn't in the facts it was given,
  • spells a number out in words (which can't be checked),
  • names a possible cause like earnings, an election or news,
  • runs too long, or
  • forgets the plain "The record:" line at the end.

Gemma gets three tries. If it still fails, the page shows a plain factual summary instead.

Even with the bigger gemma3:4b, the checker rejected 12 of 17 drafts. Many were just too long, but some were sneaky:

  • It invented share prices ("the open price was 188.73, the close 199.33") that appear nowhere in its facts.
  • Told not to write numbers as words, it turned "8.6x normal volume" into "eight hundred and sixty unseen hands".

Gemma wrote 5 of the 9 stories; the other 4 are plain summaries. A boring true sentence beats a spooky false one.

6. The page

The journal is one HTML file with no outside scripts, hosted free on GitHub Pages. I used an AI coding assistant to help write and debug the code; every run, number and story here comes from running it myself.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

It's free to run, again and again. Hundreds of model calls across my testing, with no API bill and no rate limits.

Your watchlist stays yours. The stocks you look up say a lot about you. Here nothing leaves the laptop.

I can open up every part. TabPFN gives me its full range of outcomes. When the small Gemma got numbers wrong, I swapped in a bigger one with one flag and wrapped it in my own checker, and I can read every rejected draft.

It can't be switched off. Both models are files on my disk, which felt right for a project about things that refuse to stay dead.

Who Could Use This, and How It Would Scale

Under the ghost stories is a useful idea: a surprise score for every stock, measured against its own normal. A 3% drop in a sleepy stock can mean more than 6% in a wild one, and a "top losers" list can't tell the difference. Investors could check which holdings did something truly abnormal; analysts could find the strange days first, then read the news for just those; surveillance teams look for exactly the shape of 21 November 2024, a huge unexpected move on heavy volume.

My first reader is right that nobody opens a post-mortem weekly. The version worth building is a nightly scan: one forecast per stock ("was today a ghost?") across a watchlist or a whole exchange, with Gemma writing only for the few ghosts.

What stands in the way: TabPFN-3.5's weights are non-commercial, so a paid product would need a commercial licence, and two stocks is far too little evidence.

What It Isn't

Not a trading signal and not financial advice. It tells you a day was strange, not that tomorrow will be. Moves past the forecast's edge show as "1 in 1,000+", not a precise number the model can't back up.

Code

Ghost Candles

Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

  • The Oracle: TabPFN-3.5, an open-weight tabular foundation model, runs locally. For every trading day it forecasts a full probability distribution of that day's return, using only data from before that day (walk-forward, refit every 20 days on the previous 750).
  • The Ghosts: any day whose actual move had odds of 1 in 100 or worse under the Oracle's forecast. Beyond the 0.1% / 99.9% quantiles it becomes a Wraith.
  • The Medium: a local open-weight LLM (default Google Gemma gemma3:4b via Ollama) writes a short ghost story for each one. It only gets the numbers and is told it does not know why the move happened, so it…
View on GitHub

Try it on any NSE or BSE stock:

python renarrate.py out/TATAMOTORS_NS.json --llm gemma3:4b

  • Best Use of TabPFN: TabPFN-3.5 is the Oracle. It runs locally in a no-peeking forecasting loop, its full range of outcomes decides what counts as a ghost, and it's tested honestly against a bell-curve baseline on two stocks.
